SECRET SESSION TO BE HELD ON WEDNESDAY, APRIL 17.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SECRET SESSION TO BE HELD ON WEDNESDAY, APRIL 17.
speechtext:
Having regard to the gravity of
the conditions which are confronting the Allied nations at the present time, and with the view of informing hon. members of this House in a confidential way as to certain matters upon which it is advisable that they should be informed, and as to which confidential information in regard to military exigencies could not properly be given in an ordinary session of the House, I have conferred with the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition as to the holding of ia secret session of this House. The conclusion I have reached in conjunc-

tion with my colleagues is that such a session should he held in the immediate future. It will he possible when that session is held, to explain much more in detail the reasons on account of which I think it is desirable. I therefore, move:
Resolved that the sitting of Wednesday next, the seventeenth day of April, instant, shall he a secret session until the House shall then otherwise order, and that all strangers be ordered to withdraw during such secret session ;
Provided however, that this Order shall not affect the privilege enjoyed by members of the Senate of being present at Debates in this House.
Resolved further that a message be sent to the Senate acquainting their Honours with the terms of this Resolution.
Under ordinary conditions, it is most unusual that a secret session of either House of Parliament should be held. However, during the past two years secret sessions of the British Parliament have been held on several occasions. There were two in the spring of 1916. There were two, I think, in the spring of 1917, one of which was held about the time my colleagues and I were leaving England. There was a secret session held by the British House of Commons in the month of December last and another in January. It seems desirable that under existing conditions the same course should be followed here on this occasion.

maintopic: SECRET SESSION TO BE HELD ON WEDNESDAY, APRIL 17.
speechtext: The Prime Minister, as he stated, did me the honour of consulting me last Saturday 'as to the advisability of holding a secret session of this House. The Government must, of course, take the responsibility in regard to a matter of this kind as they are in the possession of information of which the public is not aware, and it is fotr them to decide as to the advisability of conferring with Parliament in regard to it. It is also for them to decide whether, as a result of that, it will be possible to give the information to the public. But of course, all this is upon the responsibility of the Government, who have knowledge of which the public is ignorant, and which they consider the public should not have, at all events, at the present stage. Under such circumstances there can be no objection to the course the Government have decided to take. I can add to what has been said by my right hon. friend that not only has the British Parliament had secret sessions, but the French Parliament has had secret sessions on one or two occasions.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: I desire to call the attention of the House to the fact that work has been recommenced on the new parliament building, and I would consider it a very great pleasure if the members of the House would take an early opportunity of visiting the premises for the purpose of acquainting themselves with the general layout and making any suggestions which to them may seem proper with a view to expediting completion, and which might be acted upon by the committee having charge of the reconstruction. He said: Hon. gentlemen will remember that under the Bank Act banks are authorized at certain periods of the year to exceed their normal bank circulation, particularly during the period of harvesting crops in Canada. Ordinarily their note circulation is confined to their unimpaired paid-up capital, the amount of current gold accounts, and Dominion notes which they hold in the central gold reserve, which is a banking reserve. From the 1st 'September to 28th February they are permitted by the Act to issue excess circulation not exceeding 15 per cent of their paid-up capital, rest and reserve fund. Under this power the/ are obliged to pay to the Government at the rate of 5 per cent interest for such excess circulation. Section 4 of the Finance Act of 1J14 provides that the Governor in Council be further authorized to permit this excess circulation by the banks throughout the whole year; not only from the 1st of September to the let of March,~but from the let of March until the last day of August. Section 4 of the Finance Act reads :
The Governor in Council may by proclamation published in the Canada Gazette:-

The Finance Act further provides that this authority for excess circulation during the entire year, or during the addition. 1 period of six months.; (becomes effective 'by proclamation, and it always provides that the proclamation shall continue in force for not more than thirty days after the beginning of the next session of parliament, unless it has been approved by resolution passed by both houses of Parliament. Parliament opened on the 18th of iMarch, and consequently this proclamation must receive the approval of this House by resolution to-day, or possibly to-morrow. Therefore, it is, to keep perfectly within the statutory requirement, that I ask Parliament to approve of this resolution. No similar resolution was passed last year or the year before, for the reason that the proclamation issued while Parliament was in session, and the Justice Department advised the Department of Finance that the approval of Parliament was not necessary. I may say that the banks generally have exercised the powers granted under this proclamation. During the past year a total interest of $109,533.06 has been collected from the banks on account of excess note circulation. All of the chartered banks have availed themselves of the privilege given them under this provision of the Finance Act. I trust, therefore, that Parliament will be pleased to approve of the resolution. II might further say that on Friday last the 'Senate passed a resolution of approval.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. J. E. ARMSTRONG ADVOCATING DEVELOPMENT AND UTILIZATION OF FUEL RESOURCES OF CANADA.

speechtext:
Mr. JOSEPH E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is of great importance that the increased and increasing demand for fuel for manufacturing and residental purposes he supplied in larger quantities and at cheaper rates than are now possible; that the deposits of bituminous and! anthracite coal in Canada located in the extreme

eastern and western portions thereof, be more fully and thoroughly utilized for the benefit of the residents of the oentral provinces; that the enormous peat and lignite deposits so widely distributed through all portions of the Dominion be also scientifically made use of for the same purpose, and further that the Government of Canada make a special effort through legislation and otherwise, to have these valuable deposits more fully and rapidly developed to the end that the people of Canada may be adequately supplied with these fuels'.
He said: The hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. H. A. Mackie) who was- to have supported this resolution has been obliged to leave owing to illness in his family. He, therefore, asked me to read on his behalf a letter which embodies his views with respect to this resolution. The letter reads:

Ottawa, April 12ith, 1918.
__p.G your [DOT] Resolution in the House-
Hear Mr. Armstrong:-
Enclosed you will find oopy of letter which speaks for itself.	„	T
Owing to the illness of my aged father 1 arranged to go to-morrow afternoon to visit him Train connections make it impossible for me 'to return here in time for Monday's dis-*Cuss ion.
I therefore, beg you to be good enough to point out to the House, that it is possible, m my opinion, for the Provinoe of Alberta to supply all the coal needed in the Provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and even in the Province of Ontario, subject to costs and facilities of transportation.
This subject has been ably covered by Mr. Demieux, member for Maisonneuve, and I am sure he will co-operate with you in every particular. In my opinion there is no reason why the miners of Alberta should hot be kept busy at the mines during the summer months, and the coal transported and stored in such a way that only a small percentage would be lost.
If the winter demand for the Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and Manitoba is now supplied many of the miners could be transported to the Eastern coal fields, there to enlarge the output so as to supply from that point, at least the Province of Quebec, if not Ontario.	.	.
I regret very much that your Resolution is brought at this time because the delegation of miners who are coming to this city on the 17th instant, for the express purpose of discussing the ways and means of production, could be of material assistance to us in this discussion.
This Government, in my opinion, should not neglect to keep in close touch with the labour element so as to remedy, in this particular case at all events, the condition of things which exist. I would have suggestions to make, but not having had' the opportunity to discuss with the Minister of .Labour, and not knowing what he has in mind, I refrain from so doing.
Tours very truly,

The resolution which I have moved is * identically the same as that which I placed upon the Order Paper last year. It is not my intention to repeat at any great length any of the arguments which I used at that time, but I do feel that the Government should then have given this matter their immediate attention. While it is true that they have during the past ten days set aside by Order in Council the sum of $400,000 for the development of the coal areas of the West, and that they also contemplate the development of some of our enormous peat deposits, I feel that a full year has in reality been wasted, and instead of being ready with a supply of fuel for the coming winter, with its anticipated still greater shortage, we shall not be in a position to supply public demands for some considerable time unless the greatest possible speed is attained. However, I cannot but congratulate the Government upon the action they have taken, and am confident that the people of Canada will uphold them in any reasonable efforts they may make to provide fuel for the winter of 1919.
May I ask the hon. member if he will say if he knows anything of the Graham carbonizing process and if the Cabinet has taken it into consideration?

I will leave the answer to the minister; I am not positive what action they have taken. My advice to them is to speed up the organization to the utmost limit, and I am going to offer some suggestions as to how it should be

speeded up. What we need, Mr. Speaker, at the head of the Geological Survey and the Mines Branch is a man who should and would devote all his time and energy towards making it what it should be, one of the most progressive departments of this Government. He should be given a free hand to reorganize and rearrange this department. In making this statement, I do not wish in any way to criticise the present acting Minister of Mines, for I believe he is at least trying to straighten out some of the _ many things which need to be straightened out in that department; but the present Minister of Mines is also the Secretary of State, and in that position he cannot give the Department of Mines the attention it deserves during these trying days. Let me call your attention, for a moment, to the extent of the operations carried on in this department, and the amount of money which is spent.

In 1907, the Geological Survey Act was passed' and the appointment of a separate minister was considered advisable, and since that time there have been seven ministers in this department, and several acting ministers. You can readily understand, Mr. Speaker, that no definite policy could be worked out in this way. Many of these ministers did not take even a reasonable interest in their department, and some of them while they were in office never visited or inspected the branches in Ottawa to see whether those branches were living or dead-and I want to make the statement that some of the branches, at least, appear to be more dead than alive at. the present time. It is surprising to me that so much has 'been accomplished in the last few years under the circumstances. There should not 'be any divided authority in this department. I am confident that there should be a general readjustment. Some men should be superannuated; others should be dismissed, and some new blood injected into this department, which, though one of the most important, has been one of the most neglected in the service.	*	,
[Mr. J. E. Armstrong.!
There is serious overlapping in this department, and a useless waste of puJblic money as well .as of the valuable time of officials. Take the matter of statistical reports; they are one or two years old before being handed out to the public. The 1917 report has not been sent to the printer yet. Some radical changes are needed if this department is to serve the public as it should in its future development. The Minister of Manes should, at an early date, call the heads of the mines branches of each of the provinces together, and devise a scheme whereby overlapping and duplication of work should be stopped. The mines branches in the different provinces should work in perfect harmony with this department, 'but under present conditions the very opposite is the case. This department should also get in close touch with the industries using mineral products in our country, and every encouragement should be extended to assist the development of these industries. Parliament should deal generously with this branch and provide it with evgry reasonable means to carry on its work. Last year, the production of our mines amounted to over $192,000,000, of which the province of Ontario produced $71,000,000. The mines of Canada are capable of far greater development, and if the Government will take the money spent by this department in useless and unnecessary work, and add to it the money used by commissions in duplicating the work already done by this department and by the Interior Department there would be a large amount available for these developments.
Canada must be ready, after the war, to manufacture, as far as possible, her raw material. Vast quantities of raw material are leaving our mines to be manufactured into finished products in the Undted.States and elsewhere. We have only developed a small portion of our mineral area, and no country in the world can offer greater opportunities to the man who wishes to invest in mining. Canada needs a fuel controller, but she also needs a mines department that will back him up and assist him in furnishing the fuel. Why should it be necessary for the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta to import coal from Pennsylvania, two thousand miles away, when they have abundance of excellent fuel within their own boundaries? Five hundred and fifty thousand tons of Pennsylvania coal was transported to the western provinces last year, when, with proper development and distribution, the coal deposits of the West would have been quite sufficient to supply their needs. In addition to this, 2,376,934 tons of

other grades of coal from the United States were utilized in those western provinces. According to the 'Commission of Conservation, the total imports of coal into Fort William, Port Arthur and Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta points of entry for the years 1914, 1915 and 1916 were as follows: I will quote the 1916 figures:

Practically the whole province of Alberta, and many parts of Saskatchewan, are undermined with coal. These provinces have a greater quantity of coal than any country in the world with the exception of the United States. There is no excuse for a coal shortage in Canada between Port Arthur and the Pacific ocean, nor yet is there a reasonable excuse for a shortage of coal between Montreal and tha Atlantic ocean. I understand that the mines in the West would be able to materially increase production if steady employment could be given to the miners; .and by producing fuel in the. West for consumption there it would create a steady demand for coal and mean all-the-year-round operation of the mines. Millions of dollars would he kept in this country which is now going to the United States in payment for coal. The people of Nova Scotia should be furnished with transportation facilities in order to land their coal, iron, steel, coke, tar, and the chemicals produced from coal, in Quebec and Ontario ports, and in return would receive our flour, wheat, bacon and manufactured goods. Canada has tremendous resources in. her mines, and we must commence to investigate and to utilize them. The coal areas of Canada have an estimated
total extent of 109,168 square miles, and on summing up the reports of the coal deposits of the world we find that Canada has the second greatest amount available, namely,
1.234.269.000.	000 tons, while the 'United States has 3,838,659,000,000 tons available. The actual available supply in Nova Scotia is estimated at 400,000,000 tons, and the present output in that province is 5,000,000 tons per annum. The Maritime Provinces once provided the province of Quebec with
2.000.	000 tons of coal; last year they only provided 50,000 tons. It may safely be said that there will be no permanent reduction in the price of coal, rather it is reasonably certain that there will he a gradual and steady increase. The price of anthracite and other coal is advancing largely because of the exhaustion of the thicker beds, the increased cost of working and the increased freight rates. In the United States, they are digging coal dust from coal dumps and rivers, and find it, after treatment equal in many ways to the best slack coal. This .merely goes to show that the people of the United States are making every effort to conserve their fuel resources. They are also demanding that their people save fuel. In the anthracite region, during a period of many years,
5,000,000 tons- of what is called coal slush has been dumped into the rivers. If you go through that region to-day, you will see dredges working in the riveTS taking out this slush, which is afterwards sold. I understand that within the past year a considerable quantity of this material has been finding its way into 'Canada.
George H. Cushing, editor of Black Diamond, says:
The United States will start this year with 125,000 fewer miners than at the end of 1916. These men have either been drafted or have drifted to industrial centres where munition and other plants pay higher wages. Car supplies have not materially increased.
Vice-president Schayer, of the Pennsylvania railroad, after a study of the car situation says:
Only alleviation, not correction, is possible this year. It will take the railroads until the end of the war to. catch up with their traffic. Apart from direct coal requirements we must supply from American coal enough by-products to support 1,500,000 troops shooting away powder.
Let me read a paragraph from a statement made by Mr. W. J. Dick, of the Geological Survey Department, to the Mining Institute in " the * city of Montreal some-weeks ago.
Speaking of the waste of coal in Canada, W. J. E>ick said:

A large proportion of the coal mined in Canada was lost and wasted through caving [DOT]of measures owing to the practice of mining lower seams of better quality first, with the result that (by the caving in, the recovery of coal from the upper seams was generally impossible. In other countries leases were granted only on satisfaction being given the authorities that a proper scheme of operations was to be carried on. In Canada, there was indiscriminate leasing of coal lands without restriction, and if the mines were working to their capacity, the output would be 1 G,00>0,0'O'O tons per annum. He deprecated the opening up of farmer or "snowbird" mines, about 400 of which had been abandoned in Alberta alone, as they had only destroyed the entrance to a coal field for l^rge operations and were a menace to safety in the workings. He suggested that slack coal should be made into briquettes if a cheap binding could be found.
New York, April 11.-Warnings that a shortage of bituminous coal exists were issued today by fuel authorities here. The situation is so serious, according to Harry T. Peters, chairman of the State Fuel Conservation Committee, that we will be back where we were last winter unless something is done to relieve matters.
March was the worst month in point of production during the past year and a half, Mr. Peters asserted, and some factories have been forced to continue working with barely enough fuel to meet current needs.
To show how urgent is the need for conservation of coal, the following is quoted from the United States Fuel Bulletin:
But unfortunately, the transportation of coal alone uses up 30 per cent of the entire railroad equipment of the United States, cars, locomotives, sidings, and terminals.
I merely read this for the purpose of calling to the attention of the ministers the need of more stringent regulations with Tegard to the operations carried on at the mines and the development of our coal resources.
Here is a statement made )by a professor in a Saskatchewan college:
The United States wastes $500,000,000 worth of coal every year, said Dr. R. D. McLaurin, professor of chemistry at the University of Saskatchewan, in a recent letter to F. Maclure Sclanders, industrial commission of the Border Chamber of Commerce, Windsor.
Canada has been as wasteful proportionately. In view of the present necessity for fuel of all \kinds, this waste of coal is nothing less than criminal.
Let me direct the attention of hon. mem-'bexs to a statement made by H. A. Garfield, United States fuel administrator. The article is headed " Won't You Help to Save Coal?" Mr. Garfield says:
The war has created a demand upon the United States for 100,000,000 extra tons of coa.1 this year. Because of the congested condition of the railroads, due to war shipping, it will be impossible to supply more than half this additional demand through increased production alone. The remaining 50,000,000 tons needed to support war activities and to keep us warm will have to be saved shovelful by shovelful through care in American factories and homes.
The	States is called upon to produce 70 0,000,00 0 tons of coal this year. This is 100,000,000 more tons than we have ever produced before. The high water mark of production this year, in spite of all handicaps, will give 50,000,000 tons of this additional amount. The remaining 50,000,000 tons must be filled in by patriotic thriftiness. If in each home there was saved one shovelful of coal each day it would mean a total saving of 15,000,000 tons a year. Comfort for 7,500,000 soldiers in army cantonments. Enough to send a fleet of twenty-five battleships 3,00*0 miles across the Atlantic to guard our transports
This is a statement issued in New York within the last few days:

I read these extracts merely for the purpose of emphasizing horw dependent we are on the United States for a large quantity of coal annually, and the necessity of the Government taking immediate action to endeavour to supply the people of Canada with an adequate quantity of coal for the coming winter. This is a statement made by the coal operators of the Northwest:
Production in Alberta can be almost doubled in 1918 with same labour. Alberta coal operators are anxious to supply the coal needs of the Canadian West, and thus relieve the general fuel situation in Canada. To this end the Northern Alberta Coal Operators' Association has sent two delegates to Ontario to impress this on the people and through them upon the Government. There was a meeting of the coal operators of Alberta at Calgary on February 11, said Mr. Anderson, at which possibly 75 operators were present, representing the mines of Edmonton, Drumheller, Lethbridge, and the Alberta portion of the Crow's Nest Pass field. The meeting was called to ascertain what the Alberta coal mines could do to increase production in 1918. The mines of Alberta produced approximately 4,700,000 tons of coaJl in 1917. At this meeting the Crow's Nest Pass field promised an increase in 1918 over 1917 of 1,250,000 tons, Lethbridge an increase of 200,000 tons, Drumheller an increase of 1,800,000 tons, and Edmonton an increase of 1,000,000 tons, if the mines were kept running continually and with labour which is at present employed.
This country is short of transportation facilities, therefore, it is short on coal One begins to comprehend the nature of the problem when confronted with this fact: the transportation of the 30,000,000 carloads of coal mined last year constituted more than half of all the freight carried by the railroads. But when to this eloquent factor is added the explanation that railroads themselves in their locomotives used last year between 125,00*0,000 and 13(5,000,000 tons of coal, and that they will this year require for their use 175,000,000 tons, it is seen that this hauling of coal is a burdensome proposition.
During 1917 the mines of Alberta worked on an average of 13.3 days per month for the year. On February 9. when a portion of Canada was ordered to close its manufacturing concerns owing to lack of fuel, a mine in the Edmonton field, having an output of 400 to 500 tons daily,

was closed down for lack of orders. Mr. Shelden represents the Humberstone Coal Company in the same field, with an output of 800 tons daily, and which has been closed several days in February owing to lack of orders. All this while Ontario is short of fuel.
I am convinced that only by the development of our own fuel resource* in our western country can we expect to avert a crisis euch ae we had in Ontario during the last winter.
As to the question of natural gas for fuel purposes. In addition to the enormous deposits of coal, the western provinces are supplied with large quantities of natural gas; in fact, no country in the world has so large a supply. Millions of feet of this most valuable fuel are (being wasted every day- wasted, to a large extent, through the carelessness of the Mines Branch of the Interior Department, in connection with the western provinces, and wasted also through conflict between the Geological Survey and Mines Branches. I can best emphasize this statement by reading a reply to a letter I sent to the Deputy Minister of Mines. It is dated Ottawa, January 8, 1918, and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Armstrong:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where did you get that information?

From Dr.
Dowling of the Mines Branch.

speechtext: He does not know what he is talking about, if he says that.

This well has been wasting gas for the past twenty or twenty-five years; I have heard of this well myself a number of times, and have called the attention of the Mines Department to it. For years it has wasted over 500,000 feet of gas per day

an estimated loss of about one billion feet of gas altogether. There is another well on the Peace river wide open. These are only two of the wells that have been abandoned and are wasting this excellent fuel. I think the Mines Branch, so far as the leasing of wells and things of that kind is concerned, should be under the Geological Survey Branch. I think that was intended when the Act was passed on the 27th of April, 1907. Clause 4 Of that Act reads as follows:
The department shall administer all laws enacted by the Parliament of Canada relating to mines and mining, and shall also have the management and direction of all subjects assigned to it by the Governor in Council.
Whenever, under the provisions of this section, the management and direction of any subject is transferred from any other department to the Department of Mines, the Minister of Mines and the Deputy Minister of Mines shall be substituted for, and have all the powers and perform all the duties of, the minister and deputy minister, respectively, of such other department, as defined and provided by the Acts and regulations relating to such subject.
Natural gas is the cleanest and best of natural fuels. Raymond S. Blatchley of the Bureau of Mines of the United 'States estimated that up to 1914 the waste of natural gas in the state of Kansas alone had amounted to 25 billions of feet, and that the state of Oklahoma had wasted a similar amount through carelessness. Abandoned wells were improperly plugged and water was allowed to enter the gas veins. A great quantity of natural gas in the United States is being used for the manufacture of gasolene. The quantity of gasolene that may be obtained from gas ranging in specific gravity from 0-64 to 1-46 varies from zero to 5 gallons per 1,000 feet of gas. With the absorption process a natural gas containing less than 1 pint of gasolene per 1,000 feet can be treated at a profit. In the year 1915, 65,000,000 gallons of gasolene

prepared by these methods was placed on the market in the United States. The production of gasolene from natural gas in 1916 in the United States was over 100,000,000 gallons.
In order that I may give some idea of the increase of -consumption of gasolene as a fuel, the Bureau of Mines of the United States says that while the consumptiori of gasolene in 1909 was 11,000,000 barrels of 42 gallons, in 1914 it had increased to 30,000,000 barrels, in 1916 to 50,000,000 barrels, and in 1917 to 75,000,000 barrels-a total of
3,150,000,000 gallons. A similar increase in the consumption of this fuel is going on in Canada, and this is an additional reason for conserving our natural gas. The people of the United States in 1914 used 591,000,000,000 feet of natural gas in their cities, towns and factories for heating and lighting. What is Canada doing to conserve and utilize her gas fields? In Ontario, for instance, the provincial government have appointed a man whose duty it is to follow up all drilling operations in the provinces, to see that wells are carefully bored, and that no water is allowed to escape into the veins of an abandoned well through being improperly plugged.
Now a few words about powdered coal. In the United States 8,000,000 tons of powdered coal was used last year. I understand that little, if any, of this product is used in Canada.
I have made somewhat extensive inquiries in regard to the use of powdered coal in factories and on the railways, and I am convinced that we should immediately investigate the advisability of using coal in this form. In order to use coal in pulverized form it should be specially prepared, which consists of thoroughly drying -and grinding. The cost of preparation is off-set by mechanical feeding, doing away with high-priced firemen; this is particularly true when applied to firing locomotives. -It is -blown into the furnace with a burner similar to an oil burner.
I am informed that the provincial laws of Alberta forbids the burning of the high volatile lignite coal, owing to the danger from starting fires. In the pulverized form the combustion would be so thorough that there would be no danger from this source, and, besides, it entirely eliminates the smoke nuisance which is so prevalent at busy city terminals. In talking this matter over with railroad men in Alberta, they seemed to think that the high per cent of moisture in the lignite coal would seriously interfere with the burning of it in the pcwiered form. However, I have secured

There are large deposits of coal in Brazil, but it contains so great a percentage of sulphur and iron pyrites, which clinkers on the grates of -an ordinary boiler, that it was impossible to get results, and for this reason had practically no commercial value.
The Brazilian Government, learning that their native coal might be used in the powdered form, sent Dr. Ri-berio, Locomotive Superintendent of the Central Kailway of Brazil, to the United States to make a test of 50 tons of Brazilian coal on locomotives in- the pulverized form, analysis of which was as follows :

The American Locomotive Works at Schenectady, N.Y., have a powdered fuel plant, and they are using this form of fuel

I submit this information to the House ' for its consideration.
Now, in regard to electricity. The simplest way to cut dawn our coal imports into Ontario is to use our water-powers, when Niagara and the St. Lawrence, and their tributaries are doing the work they should do there will be little need of coal for industrial development, we will however need large quantities of coal for heating purposes. What is the Dominion doing to assist in the development of electricity? Should we leave the development of this industry to the provinces? Ontario for instance, has $50,000,000 invested in the electrical development of the province. It is estimated that Canada has 18,800,000 horsepower available from her water-powers, and has only developed 1,800,000 horse-power, leaving about seventeen million horse-power undeveloped. (Assuming a horse-power to call on an average of 10 tons of coal per annum.) This means a waste of 170,000,000 tons of coal annually, providing it was necessary to develop all our water-powers. What are we doing as a Dominion to control this enormous waste? If we did not have the development of electricity in Canada we would be compelled to import from the United States or other countries double the amount of coal we are importing to-day. Canada has the greatest amount of waterpower in any country in the world, and in the future there will be tremendous developments in this direction. This Government should place the development of electricity for light, heat, and power purposes, under some minister who will take an active interest in its promotion.
Just a word in regard to our peat deposits. *It is not m'y intention to discuss at any length the question of peat, oil shale, deposits, or producer gas. The Government officials decided that peat could be manufactured in blocks suitable for industries and private homes at an actual cost of $1.75 per ton. The officials of the Mines Branch . claim that this was the actual cost per ton of producing 2,000 tons from the Alfred bog, just outside Ottawa. If the officials
of the Government are correct in their calculations as to the cost of this peat, we are neglecting the development of our peat 'bogs. Canada has 37,000 square miles of known peat bogs, but these form probably but a small fraction of the total constituting a potential national asset of enormous value. The peat deposits of Canada are greater in extent than those of any other country with the exception of Russia. During the period from 1908 to 1914 the Mines Branch located, mapped and investigated 140,000 acres of bogs, estimated to be capable of yielding 115,000,000 tons of fuel, and 10,500,000 tons of peat moss litter. Seven, of these bogs within convenient shipping distance of Toronto, will yield 26,500,000 tons of fuel, four 'bogs within a few miles of Ottawa are estimated to contain over 25 million tons. Seven bogs in the Montreal district could furnish that city with 23,500,000 tons of fuel, and five bogs along the St. Lawrence and convenient to Quebec, could supply 16,250,000 tons of fuel. Next winter there will be a greater demand for fuel, and the railroads cannot cope with the conditions, and handle any great quantities of this fuel. We are calling for greater production, and the railroads will be taxed to their utmost. How then can we expect to be in a better position as regards transportation? This is the time to begin to speed up coal delivery, and to urge the production of other fuels as well as coal. The Department of Mines of the United States issues a pamphlet, called "Five ways of saving fuel in heating houses."
We should educate our people in the use of lower grades of fuel. The same department issues another pamphlet called "Firing bituminous coal in house heating boilers." We educate our people in food conservation, why not in fuel conservation? A campaign of publicity, through the press and otherwise, should be instituted similar to the campaign for food conservation. Farmers, and others living in rural communities, should be urged to use wood fuel. Canada must plan for a fuel supply, not only for this year or next year, but for generations to come. The coal shortage of the United States last year was officially estimated to be 50,000,000 tons. The people of Canada in 1916 used 30,000,000 tons of coal and we only produced 14,500,000 tons.
There will be far greater shortage this year unless immediate action is taken. The demands for coal for industrial purposes have greatly increased, and the demands for export purposes have increased enormously. The United States, through its fuel administration, has ordered that no

coal is to be exported from that country except to Canada. How long will the United States deplete her stock of coal to keep us warm and to keep the wheels of our enterprises going? The coal shortage in the United' States will continue for the duration of the war and Canada is sure to he seriously affected thereby. Canada to-day is facing a fuel situation of great gravity, a situation created by our dependence on the United States for our fuel supply. It will be quite impossible for that country to supply our needs, and1 give reasonable attention to the requirements of her people.
Our present position is most unsatisfactory and can only be improved by a determined and energetic exploitation and utilization of our own vast fuel resources. To do nothing, or to waste time, must lead to misery and disaster. Drastic measures must be undertaken by this Government in order to prevent as far as possible a serious shortage of fuel in 1919. I therefore respectfully urge that every effort be put forth by this Government to provide for abundance of fuel for the coming winter, and at the same time lay the foundation for an unlimited supply of fuel for the future.
I should like to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) if he could give us the comparative figures as to the export of coal from the United States to Canada and from Canada to the United States.
I regret I am not in a position to give those figures. I have no doubt the minister will be very glad to supply that information.

Mr. Speaker, provided that this House gives assent to the resolution that is proposed by my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), and the Government gives effect to it. it will be of such inestimable value to the section of country in which I live, that I feel I would be derelict in my duty if I did not give as strongly as I can my support to the resolution. I have referred to the section of the country in which I live, and I hope that my hon friend from Lambton will forgive me for taking a sectional view of what is a splendid Dominion-wide policy. If anything which I feel in connection with this policy is not any larger than the section or the province I represent I do not think the point which I propose to make would be worthy of respect. This is a Dominion wide policy and I hope that, while I am 
speaking of the section I represent, no one will feel that I am too small a man to take a broad view of the question.
The section of the country to which I refer is the whole east half of the province of Saskatchewan and a large portion of the province of Manitoba, in which territory, there live at least one million people and the coal supply for that one million people should naturally come from the lignite fields of Southern Saskatchewan. I believe I am correct when I say that from these fields can be taken, not millions of tons of coal, but billions upon billions of tons. I believe, so enormous is that coal field, that it will supply Canada for hundreds of years to come. Notwithstanding the fact that we have one million people living there, and notwithstanding the fact that there .are billions of tons of coal, we are using only two hundred thousand tons a year out of that field.
To-day I am somewhat in a state of doubt, not in regard to the resolution, because I give it my most hearty endorsement, but in regard to my attitude towards governmental action. Doubt has come to me because of the statement which was made in this House last week by the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), in reply to the motion made by the hon. member from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). I paid particular attention to him as he was speaking and I noticed that he spoke with a great deal of hesitancy. I know the Minister of the Interior and I know that hesitancy is not one of his characteristics. I also noticed that he was lacking in detail upon that particular occasion. I know that he is a master of detail and I rather wondered at that. I also noticed that he was not too definite in what he said and he usually is quite definite. So, I came to the conclusion, which I think was natural, that the hon. member was not too sure himself of the question upon which he was 'speaking. Then, in the last two. or three days, taking up the western press, I have noticed that they have been dealing with his statement very extensively and I find that they are very much in doubt .as to what is proposed. Some of them say that the Government has decided to vote $200,000 for the development of the lignite fields of -southern Saskatchewan and that the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan would each vote $100,000, making $400,000, . and that this was to be used in establishing a briquetting plant at Estevan. Then again, the press informed us that they had interviewed the local governments and that

the local governments had expressed themselves to the effect that they did not know anything about it. We are informed by the hon. member for Lambton that an Order in Council appropriating $400,000 has been passed. I hope that is so, and I hope that my ignorance in regard to the matter may be excused. I have never seen that Order in Council, but as the whole thing appears to be in a state of doubt, I feel that I should support, just as strongly as I can, the resolution of my hon. friend from Lamb-ton, and urge upon the Government that if they have not yet decided to vote that money, they should immediately decide to do so.
About ten days ago the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell), from his seat in this House, made a statement, which 1 took to be an enunciation of policy on the part of the Government, when he said that not one dollar of money would be expended on any unnecessary work. I take that to be a hint to all members of this House that we need not bother ourselves very much asking for local improvements. With that policy I fully agree. The seventy thousand people living in the constituency of Regina have sent me down here for one purpose, and one purpose only, and that is to remove all embarrassments from the Government of Canada until we had got this accursed war out of the way. That is the reason I am here. I am not here to make any unusual demands and I do not intend to do so. But at the same time I can say that this $400,000 would not be an expenditure at all, but it would be an investment which would return the full amount to the Government and to the people, because they are one, and under those circumstances I think I am justified in saying that such an expenditure would be entirely within the policy announced by the Minister of Public Works.
Why is it that only two hundred thousand tons of lignite coal have been mined and used annually in that section, and why is it that we are importing, as the hon. member from Lambton has said, .some five hundred thousand tons of anthracite from Pennsylvania? Surely Saskatchewan is not a natural market for the anthracite of Pennsylvania? I believe most thoroughly in the policy of the exchange of products, and is not coal a commodity in Tegard to which an exchange can naturally be made? The mines of the maritime provinces might find their natural market in the eastern United States, and the United States might send us their coal without hindrance. But
when it comes to Saskatchewan, I cannot imagine any one saying that Saskatchewan is the natural market for anthracite from the Pennsylvania coal fields, when we have billions of tons of coal in our own territory. Why, then, is it that it- is being sent there? I think some of the hon. members of the House will be interested in knowing the results of the experiments which were made in the city of Regina last year because of the coal shortage, and the result of which will show that governmental action is absolutely necessary and advisable, and would be profitable if it were undertaken. Last year, in connection with our municipal power plant, we entered into a contract for twenty thousand tons of Greenhill coal, and Greenhill coal is the finest coal that is mined on earth, and it comes from the province of Alberta. But the Government authorized the breaking of the contracts, with the result that we had to increase the price. More than that we were confronted with, the possibility of not getting coal at all. So we decided to authorize our commissioners to purchase two thousand tons of this lignite coal to use in our plant as an experiment in order to see how it would compare with the other coal, and whether it could (be used advantageously or not. Now, I will give you some of the results of that test in order to demonstrate what the conditions are, and to show you that governmental action is necessary if we are going to be able to use the coal from this, immense coal field.
Where did you get your lignite?

From Estevan, which is
ninety miles, as the crow flies, from our city. As I .say, we agreed to purchase twenty thousand tons of western coal, which had to be brought a distance of six hundred miles to Regina. The Estevan mines are only ninety miles, as the crow flies, south of Regina, but when we came to purchase the Estevan coal we found that in order to get it to Regina-and the same thing applies to the natural market for this coal-we had to bring it to our city in a very roundabout way. Instead of it being a matter of ninety miles, we had to ship the coal west and then double -back, involving a distance of one hundred and fifty miles all told. The freight rate for the six hundred mile journey required to bring the Greenhill coal from the Alberta mines to Regina was $3 a ton, whereas; the freight rate from Estevan by the roundabout way of a hundred and fifty miles was $1.50 a ton.



That is to say, bringing in the Estevan coal by the roundabout way cost twice the rate per ton per mile involved in bringing in the Alberta coal. Hon. gentlemen will readily see that is a very great handicap indeed. I would point out to the Minister of the Interior and to the Minister of Finance that in order to make their investment of $400,000 in coal development a profitable one, it will foe necessary to build a seven-mile railway from the Grand Trunk Paejfic railway in order to tap these mines. In that way a direct line from 'the mines to the natural market will foe provided. I do not know what interest the present Government has in the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, but I fancy that sooner or later it will have a very substantial interest in the deficits of that line, and the easiest way to get rid of those deficits would be to build the little spur line which I have suggested and this would permit of the public getting ample supplies of coal by direct route.
What would that make your distance to the mines?

Less than one hundred miles. It would save about sixty or seventy miles and make the distance to be covered between ninety and one hundred miles. .The building of the suggested seven-mile spur would give easy access to the whole of the north and north east country, and bring these coal mines into direct communication with the natural market.
Well, we found that not only did we have to pay double freight rates on this lignite, but when we came to experiment with it we proved conclusively that it carried a water content of thirty-one per cent. Now the usual water content for the western Alberta coal is less than two- per cent, so hon. gentlemen will see how we were handicapped. We had to pay double freight rates on coal thirty-one per cent of which was water, and the House will readily understand it is a rather difficult thing to burn water.
There is evidently as much water in the coal itself as there is in the stock of some of these coal companies.

If the hon. gentleman is inviting me to express an opinion about water in the stock of some of the coal companies I might be inclined to say some very harsh things, but I will not do that at present. In addition to having thirty-one per cent of water in this coal, we found ourselves further handicapped when we

came to burn it; it took eleven per cent of the heat of the coal to drive out the thirty-one per cent of water content already there. Hon. gentlemen will therefore see that we were handicapped from the beginning with a forty-two per cent loss. Even in the face of all these handicaps we found we could use this coal with a loss of only eighteen cents per ton, which proved to me conclusively that if we could secure one or two things we might use it with success. Those things are: To get a direct route so that the freight rates would be computed on the shortest route to point of 'destination, or a reduction equivalent tr the rate per ton per mile obtainable on the main line.
Now what can we do to remedy the existing state of affairs, and that is the question, I think, which confronts the Government to-day if it is going into the development of our coal resources? We thought probably we could dry this coal, and if can be dried pretty conveniently, but when you have the dried product you have a rather dangerous commodity; it is very explosive, as a matter of fact, and I would not care to recommend it. In addition to that, after the lignite is dried and left exposed for any length of time, we found that in twenty-four hours it again carried a water content of twelve per cent, having absorbed that amount of moisture from the air during one day. It is therefore evident that the drying of the coal is not sufficient to meet the difficulty. There is one thing that can be done, however, and that is briquette the coal, for it can be briquetted very successfully. I am not speaking of my own knowledge on this point, I have before me the report of the Government of the province of Saskatchewan, which has gone into the subject pretty extensively. In quoting this report, I do not wish to he accused of being actuated by party or political bias. The Government of Saskatchewan has, ever since the province was created, been of the Liberal persuasion, and I have always been -at least until the war broke out-a very ardent Tory, and I certainly am not ashamed of it. I am therefore not speaking with any party bias, and I can say-notwithstanding the fact that the Government of Saskatchewan is always wrong, except when it is right-that the reports which it publishes are quite reliable, and the report in question not only contains a good deal of common sense, but displays evidences of enterprise. In the matter of briquetting the Government's investigations have been very extensive. Their tests were not merely

laboratory tests, although they have carried those out of course, hut they have sent a very substantial quantity of this lignite coal to places where briquetting is done, and brought it back, and they have given the product the most severe test which could be given. They use a certain quantity of the briquettes in their own plant built for the purpose, and the balance of it was distributed in small lots among several hundred families of the province, in order to be tested in domestic circles. 'I think you will agree with me that if this fuel is to be used 'by the people for domestic purposes that was the proper kind of test to give it; to send it out amongst the people and let them test it for themselves, and let their opinion prevail. I have a great deal of faith in public opinion, and when that public opinion comes back in the form in which it. has here, and in the shape of reliable Government reports, we must accept that opinion. The conclusion was that the briquettes had given entire satisfaction. Now if we can briquette this coal for several hundred families and give entire or universal satisfaction I think I am safe in saying that we can briquette it for several thousand families, and also give universal satisfaction. If it can be done* and it has been done on a small scale, why can we not do it in a more extensive way, and thus save ourselves from importing these hundreds of thousands of tons into an unnatural market? I will read one or two extracts from the report to which I have referred, which will show conclusively that this is a very sound proposition.
The briquettes made from the Saskatchewan carbonized lignite have 11,500 to 12,000 British thermal units per pound. They burn with a short flame, no odour, no smoke (except a very little resulting from the volatilizing of some of the pitch binder when first thrown on the fire), and no clinker. They can be used wherever anthracite or bituminous coal is burned. They retain their structure in the fire until completely consumed. They do not disintegrate or lose value in the weather, and can therefore be stored for any length of time and shipped any distance without loss.
Now, I want to know what better product for use by our people you could have than that?
They do not disintegrate or lose value in the weather, and can therefore be stored for any length of time and shipped any distance without loss.
That makes it a staple product, and if it can be produced in quantities at a commercial rate, I say that the proper thing for our 'Government to do is to immediately provide it. The article goes on:
48*
As a domestic fuel they are fully equal to the anthracite that is marketed here ton for ton. While the anthracite averages approximately 13,000 British thermal units per pound, a little higher than the lignite briquettes when compared in a laboratory, there is no clinker from the lignite briquettes, no loss in burning, and they can be used nicely in kitchen ranges, which ds impracticable with hard coal. They make an exceptionally fine fuel for fireplaces.
And in another place, I find this:
Carbonized Lignite Briquettes. -These have proved excellent for domestic service and are equal in fuel value, ton for ton, to the anthracite marketed in this territory.
Now, I need not proceed further, I think that you will agree that that is sufficient proof that this is a practicable process.
What is meant by carbonized briquettes? Is it the raw coal passed through a press?

Yes, it is passed through
a press. That is what I am urging, that these presses be -adopted; that is what we want to have established there. I will just refer to that here.
What is the hinder used in making these briquettes?

They have been experimenting with a number of binders. The one which they are using makes an absolutely safe briquette. There is very little pitch in it, so that there is no odour. When they are first thrown on the fire there is a bright flame, lasting only a moment or two. I am speaking from personal knowledge, because I have 'burned them in my own house. They burn until completely burned out.
To find out whether this is a commercial proposition or not. You can establish as many units as you wish. One unit will cost some $75,000, that is, it would have cost about that when this report was issued, but I suppose the price will be somewhat increased now, for in the last year and -a half the cost of everything has increased very substantially. But a $75,000 unit will produce in one year 50,000 tons of briquettes. The $400,000 which is now to be expended could establish, as I understand it, about five of these units, and of course, you could add as many units as you saw fit. Would that be a pTofitaible thing to do?-to spend $75,000 to produce fifty thousand tons of briquettes? You may look at in this way: I will begin 'by taking the city in which I live as an example. In that city, fortunately, it so happens that we use fifty thousand tons, or thereabouts, every year, of Pennsylvania anthracite coal, so that we consume an amount equal to what would
I

be produced by one of these units. That ooal sells in Regina to-day at $15 a ton. As a matter of fact, it is such an inferior quality of coal which we are now getting that, compared with the price paid two or three years ago, we must be paying between $22 and $25 a ton for it; the coal is really not fit to be imported into that country at all. The excess freight rate from Pennsylvania to Regina-by that I mean the amount of freight on this coal additional to what it would be if shipped from Estevan to Regina-is a little over $4 a ton. So that we are paying $200,000 per year in freight rates alone over what we would pay if we got the coal from our own mines one hundred miles away. Is it profitable to spend $75,000 .and thereby save in one year the sum of $125,000, which is the difference in freight rates, and at the end of the year be possessed of the plant which has been established?
But it is not only that. The hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) drew attention to the fact that there was a very keen coal shortage in eastern Canada last year. I do not think that there was so much a coal shortage as a shortage of freight cars, engineers and conductors. If I mistake not, the shortage was in- the matter of transportation. Now, let us look at it that way. We in Saskatchewan .are two thousand miles away from the Pennsylvania coal fields; we are three times as far away from the anthracite mines as they are in the central part of the province of Ontario. Now, take the fifty thousand tons of coal .and multiply it by three, making 150,000 tons, representing the increased poesi-ble haulage, and you will have some idea of the number of cars that would be available to ship coal to the settled portions of the province of Ontario. Or, take the 500,000 tons of coal delivered annually in the provinces of Manitoba and *Saskatchewan, and multiply it in the same way, and the result is 1,500,000 tons. Would the release of that transportation have been of any value to the province of Ontario last winter, or it may he, in the coming year? That is the question. If you can remove the loss due to the long transportation, cut it in three, and enable the transportation officers to concentrate their attention upon delivering coal to their nearest or natural market, you will have done something well worth while in the matter of assisting our country at this particular stage of its history. I do not know that I can add anything more to this subject, excepting, in a general way, to give
[Mr. Cowan. 1
strong support to the resolution which the hon. member for Lambton moved. I cannot imagine why these coal fields were put in Canada unless to be developed by the Canadian people. I cannot imagine what the Canadian people are in Canada for unless it is to develop the natural resources of the Dominion. Anything short of that falls far below the ideal of a genuine Canadian policy, and for that reason I support this resolution as strongly as I can.

In my own plant, I am using only about 120 h.p., but the rental of the space that it would take to put in a 120 h.p. boiler and engine would be more than what I pay for that power for the year. I presume my experience does not differ very much from that of many others. This development, which after all is a fuel development, has been of inestimable value to the people of Ontario. If the conditions in the Mines Branch are as bad as the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. I have no knowledge of the matter myself, but certainly the importance of the work to be done by that branch makes it advisable for us to take steps to make it efficient, because this is going to be one of the big questions before the Dominion of Canada, not only at the present but in the future.
Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Maison-neuve),: Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion this afternoon, and I will re-echo the statement of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) that I too am sorry the House is so depleted when such a vital question is being debated. It is true we have extremely fine weather to-day, but only a few weeks ago there was a great deal of misery, suffering and hardship in this city of Ottawa. As I said the other day in presenting a motion on similar lines, the summer will soon pass away, and the same hardships will be felt throughout the central part of Canada. Sir, the House and the Government especially should recognize the emergency and face the issue squarely, and take proper measures to save the country from the consequences of another more

serious fuel shortage which may confront us next winter.
I am not exaggerating at all when I say that central Canada-the province of Ontario and a large part of the province of Quebec-is absolutely dependent on the United States for coal. The West can take care of itself, and so can the extreme East, Nova iSIcotia, Cape Breton and the Mari-ime Provinces generally, but Central Canada is absolutely dependent on Pennsylvania. The fuel controller in the United States has just issued a statement in which he says: " the United States is short in transportation facilities, and therefore it is short in coal." Then he gives a series of figures and averages, and concludes by saying that the war has created a demand upon the United for 100,000,000 tons of coal more this year than is normally produced. Because of the car shortage and the congested condition of the roads it will be impossible to increase the supply by more than 50,000,000 tons. The remaining 50,000,000 tons will have to be filled in by conservation in the homes and industrial plants of America.
That explains why our cars are kept on the other side.

There is a shortage of cars and a shortage of labour. As I said the other day, this emergency exists because of war conditions and because, of a lack of transportation facilities and the labour situation. As it does exist in the United States, our chief source of supply, we in Canada must look around and see v/hat can be done for next winter. The coal shortage last winter was felt in many hemes and industrial plants, and . though I do not wish to be unduly pessimistic, it will be more severe next winter. What is the Government going to do about it? My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce- has passed the Daylight Saving Bill; that is a step forward, but there is still something to be done. The Government have appointed a fuel controller, the best available man in the country. Mr. Magrath is a conscientious and most painstaking gentleman, and I am sure he will do his duty. My hon. friend from Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) has given us his theories about the briquetting of lignite in the West. Whilst I admit the value of these experiments, still they are only experiments, and in this emergency the country cannot afford to wait on experiments, I saw in the press the_ other day that the Government has voted $400,000 to experiment with briquetting lignite coal in the

W-est, and I am pleased if that is true; but as my hon.- friend from Toronto said a moment ago, there is something more to do. Perhaps removing the d-uty on coal during the war would help, but that, is not the point I wish to make just now. The point is this: the Government, in addition to encouraging as much as possible the conservation of coal, should also encourage the intensified production of wood fuel for next winter. I read a letter in the Ottawa Citizen not long ago from a man who is certainly an authority on that qfiestion;
I refer to Senator Edwards. He said that in this country there are such large forest reserves that in view of thq coal famine next winter the Dominion Government should bring about a more intense production of wood for fuel purposes. That is what they are doing in the United States.
I see that a conference has been called by Mr. J. J. Storrow, the federal fuel administrator for New England, who says:
A serious shortage of coal threatens New England this winter. The situation does not warrant neglecting any possible measure of preparedness. For this reason it seems advisable to make a New England campaign for the production of wood on a large scale. Good hardwood properly prepared and dried can be used extensively for domestic purposes as an emergency measure. Wood cut in November can be burned the latter part of the winter, when the coal situation may be more acute. The campaign should also look ahead toward a large supply of wood for next winter when the coal situation may be more serious than this year.
Here we have the fuel administrator for New England saying that in his section of the United States, not so far from Pennsylvania, they will have to look for a more intense production of wood fuel to replace the coal they will be short of within a few months. If that is the condition in New England, surely there is all the more reason for us in central Canada to produce more wood. We have mill waste, generally speaking, in the large centres, but we all know that the production of the mills has been reduced considerably of late. The farmers, too, are not making such a large cut as formerly, because they are much more interested in their crops this year. There is, besides, the further handicap of lack of transportation facilities. I believe that the Government, jointly with Mr. Magrath, should have a forestry inspector appointed to encourage concurrently with the conservation of coal, the production of wood for next winter's fuel. This could be done by first of all encouraging the municipal authorities, on the lines adopted in Ottawa and Winnipeg last winter, to accumulate a reserve of wood fuel. Then there should be
a commission of publicity directed by the fuel controller to restrain people from using coal between the ,15th of April and the 15th of December. The farmers should be eu-couraged to make a larger cut, and the provincial governments should be asked to assist materially from the Crown lands. There is no doubt that the emergency exists.
I also agree with the remarks of my hon. friend from Toronto in regard to the water-powers of this country. While I do not wish to discuss what some people call the confiscatory policy which is laid at the door of the Ontario Hydro Commission, 1 must say that the policy of the province of Ontario with regard to water-powers is very commendable, and I should like to have this Government see that the water-powers of this country are conserved for the consumers of Canada. I was surprised the other day to read of the enormous'amount of power that could be developed in and around the- city of Montreal. Our water-powers constitute one, if not the biggest, asset of Canada. The Montreal Herald says:
Montreal has an enormous source of supply right at her doors. For instance there is the supply developed at the Cedar Rapids. Although this supply is developed In Canadian territory 65,000 horse power, out of a total of lOO.OOo'h. p., is being exported to the United States. "Few people," says Mr. White," have any conception of what the 65,000 h.p., now being exported to the United States from the Cedars, could do if widely distributed to customers of light and power. In 1916 a little less than 50,000 h.p., met the requirements for light and power of the 40,000 customers of the Toronto Hydro-Electric Power Commission. Including the requirements of the Toronto Street Railway, the Toronto Electric Light Company, and the Toronto Hydro-Electric Power Commission, 120,000 h.p., is now required for light and power in the municipality of Toronto. Therefore, the 65,000 h.p., exported from the Cedars would, if retained in Canada, supply, at cheap rates all the light and power required for a manufacturing city of 300,000 inhabitants. If distributed through Canadian municipalities it would supply light and power to some 35 manufacturing cities of 10,000 inhabitants each; or it would practically take care of one-third of the present demands of the Niagara system of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, which supplies over 100 municipalities and 100,000 purchasers of electricity.
The water-power development in Canada has been marvellous, and I am pleased to say that in my own province of Quebec it ha-s, been on a par with that in Ontario. Those of you who have lately visited the St. Maurice valley must have been surprised at the number of industries whjch have been established in that distriet, due to the intelligent work done by the Quebec government in conserving the water-powers of that

river. Reading a report of the Laurentide Company, I observed that the president, Mr. Aldred, stated that some industries, which formerly had manifested a desire to establish themselves not far from the Niagara power, bad changed their plans, and were now establishing themselves at Shaw-inigan and Grand Mere. My hon. friend knows these facts. It shows that with a comprehensive and aggressive water-power policy, a government can accomplish much. I say that by giving free hand to our fuel controller by a very aggressive campaign of publicity, we may conserve our coal; by the appointment of a forestry inspector, so as to accentuate the production of wood next winter, and, by adopting the policy of conserving and developing our water powers in the interest of the Canadian consumer, w.e may still be able to face the emergency of the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong), has brought up a resolution dealing with a subject of great interest to this House and the country, as he did last year, when he made a very valuable address to this House which was fully discussed. The gist of his resolution is that there should be more rapid and scientific development of our resources, and of our fuel .supply, and especially in this time of war, the Government should take speedy action to utilize all the resources; and, as far as the resolution is directed to that end, I think the Government must be strongly in accord with its terms. My hon. friend ventured on somewhat severe criticisms of the department over which I have the honour to preside at the present time. I am quite convinced that any criticism which has been directed at the department were only designed to strengthen the weak spots that existed, and I am quite sure he did not intend his remarks to be taken as seriously as they appear to be taken by the hon. gentleman from South Toronto (Mr. Hocken), who suggested the appointment of a committee. I have had the honour of being Minister of Mines for a comparatively short period, and at the time when I took charge of that department it was decided to make a general appeal to the country and the ministers were called upon to leave their posts at Ottawa and absent themselves for several months. I do not think the hon. gentleman would imagine that under those circumstances the minister would be able to become quickly settled in the administration of so large a department. I wish to assure my hon. friend from Lambton that,

*in spite of the facts which I have stated, I can conscientiously say that I have given a considerable portion of my time and energy to the Department of Mines, which I think is of immense importance to the country, and which should render an enormous service to the country at all times, and especially in times of war. I am in accord with the hon. gentlemen that there is. a certain amount of duplication in the department in reference to mining matters. Probably that is the case with all departments under democratic forms of Government. I would not have to go far afield to illustrate that. However, it should be our absolute duty to cut out these duplications, as far as we can, and corelate the work of the departments in such a way that there would be no waste of energy, for, I assure my hon. friend, I will endeavour to do my duty as far as my department is concerned. I wish to assure him we are endeavouring to keep in touch with what is being done by the provincial governments, and in other ways in the country. I had the pleasure of attending the meeting of the Mining Institute in Montreal, at which gentlemen from all parts of the country interested in mines were present, and very valuable discussions took place, in which we came in touch firsthand with the people doing the work from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I would also point out that we have kept in touch with the broader aspects of these matters. There has been, during the last two or three years, a good deal of legislation and discussion in the British Parliament in regard to minerals and mineral legislation. They are now forming what is 'known as the Imperial Mineral Resources Bureau, dealing with all the work of all the governments in the Empire, and with the endeavour, as far as possible, to keep within the Empire a control, as' far as possible, of all the minerals essential for the war, and they asked us to send over a representative (to act on the advisory board of that bureau. After taking the matter up with the Mining Institute and other bodies from other governments, we decided to send over a gentleman from Ontario, Dr. Miller, provincial geologist, a man of very wide information, a geological and mining expert, who will render a great service to Canada, when he goes over to represent Canada on that board. May I say to the House that the Department of Mines was only created as recently as 1907. The Geological Survey, which is now a part of the Department oif Mines, has, of course, been in existence for a long time, in fact, since 1842. Six provinces own their Crown lands and

deal with all these matters of administration and legislation in connection with the Crown lands and the minerals of their respective provinces. In Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and in the railway-belt of British Columbia matters are different, because the Crown lands are in the Federal Government, and the Federal Government has to do, therefore, with the minerals and the Crown lands. But the administration of those have been left, and always were left, in the hands of the Department of the Interior. Therefore, the Department of Mines, as it exists now, and as it was created in 1907, is not administrative in character. I make no pronouncement as to whether some of the functions of the Department of the Interior should be handed over to the Department of Mings or not-I am not dealing with that question now-but I want to point out to the House that the work of the Department of Mines is not administrative 'but is investigational and educational exclusively in character.
'The Geological Survey, a very important part of the Department of Mines, deals of course with the occurrence in various districts of minerals, secures accurate information in regard to our mineral resources in the way of exploration. Where development has taken place there are a large number of requests for detailed information and detailed work, such as deciphering the local geology, structure of ore deposits and problems connected' with their form and extent and other work of a geological character. Anybody who knows the western country knows what happened in the great camp at Rossland. When they thought that they had practically exhausted their ore bodies at a certain level, owing to the work of the Geological Survey they discovered- that larger bodies could be successfully developed at lower levels and since that time, largely due to the work of the Geological Survey, there has been a marvellous development in that camp.
' Half of the work of the department, as it is done at this time, is practically concerned with problems of the war. The department is devoting itself to the working out of problems that are placed before it, sometimes by the Imperial Munitions Board and sometimes by the War Trade Board or other bodies. I could give one or two illustrations. In connection with ferro alloys, the laboratory work of the officers of the Mines Department has been such that the British Government -and the War Office accept the decisions and judgments of those officers
in connection with the selling and purchases of ferro alloys in Canada. In the chemical division there is a lot of very valuable work going on in connection with the analysis of fuel values of coal, of lignite, oil shales, peat, etc., and also in connection with the testing and analysis of gases from coal. There are other things that I would like briefly to touch upon that are important at this time. We are now endeavouring to make an effort to discover additional sources of platinum. The platinum supply of the world has been practically derived from the Ural mountains in Russia and that supply has, of course, been absolutely cut off during the war. Platinum, as hon. gentlemen know, has a value about five times that of gold1 and it is getting so scarce that the war authorities in all the allied countries are getting somewhat seriously alarmed. There is very little in the United 'States, there is hardly any in Canada and comparatively few ounces produced. Some of this has been discovered in the nickel matte from Sudbury in the refining process carried on. A small amount occurs in the ultra basic rocks in British Columbia and a small amount in some of the nuggets recovered from the placer diggings in the creeks of that province. We hope to make a special investigation of this work and have detailed some of our officers to examine the rocks in place in the hope of, if possible, getting a greater production of platinum which is an imperative necessity in connection with the war.
Pulp manufacturers have had great difficulty in getting suitable stone for their business. It was imported formerly by them. We have investigated carefully a large number of quarries to ascertain *whether the stones in those quarries were suitable for this purpose and as a result we have brought the quarry owners into touch with the manufacturers of stones and have been instrumental in seeing a very large number of orders placed for pulp stones which were formerly brought from other countries.
I need not touch on other matters not directly connected with the war tout which are of immense value to the country because the department is not only devoting itself to work in connection with the war but also to work which will be of importance in peaceful times after the war. We are taking up very vigorously the question of road materials. At the request of the provincial governments of Canada we are making an investigation of and testing an enormous number of the different road de-
