speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I was just coming tothat point. In 1910 or 1911, operations were discontinued. The price of anthracite then was very much lower than it is at the present time, and the difficulties in connection with the problem-to demonstrate that peat fuel could be manufactured-having been solved, the department deemed its work to be done. It was thought proper not to proceed further, but to leave the rest to private enterprise. In the summer of 1911 a large part of 'the plant was taken over by Mr. Shuttleworth of Brantford, who also approached the Government with a view of purchasing the bog and the railway siding in order to erect an improved peat manufacturing plant. These were transferred to him in 1912, and he then began the construction of a mechanical excavator to do away with hand labour, hoping thereby to place the enterprise on a more economical basis. Mr. Shuttleworth constructed a mechanical excavator after the design of A. Anrep, Sr., of Sweden', who had been identified with peat development in Russia and Sweden for thirty or forty years, and his plant was

finally ready for operation in 1913. It is too long a story to go into the whole of these details, but the gentleman who advanced the money for this enterprise went to England. In 1914 the war broke out. The promoters could not get sufficient capital, and, although for a certain time the manufacture of peat was successfully undertaken, a certain number of defects developed in the machinery, and owing to the shortage of capital and other conditions the company at last went into liquidation, and the bog was again sold. The bog and some of the plant was taken over >by a syndicate which is still in possession. That was the position of affairs up to this winter.
It seemed to me, therefore, when the matter was brought to my attention, and considering the mounting price of anthracite, and the severity of a winter like last which brought home the fuel question to every one's mind in a startling way, that it was desirable to look into this more thoroughly; and for that reason we took the-peat question up again, because the main difficulty in the way was the great expense of handling it and the absolute necessity of finding some kind of improved peat machinery that would do away with the large aipount of hand labour, the whole question coming down, not to the matter of being able to make fuel-we can do that beyond question-but of handling the raw material, in the cheapest possible way, of getting it to the point of consumption so that it could reasonably compete with anthracite. With that idea, I consulted with Mr. R. A. Ross, the engineering expert who is on the advisory council, and with the experts in my own department, and later on I found that the Government of Ontario was very keen on the same subject and we went into the whole thing with them, and had a conference or two, the result of it simply being this: we came to the conclusion that it would be desirable to have two types of peat machines, or what we may call units, first, to take again the old plant that was used in 1911, which was based on the Anrep design, and improve it as far as . it could be improved, utilizing such methods as were utilized at that time; and, in the second place, to try and bring out some entirely new type of machine, which Mr. Moore, the engineer who had been associated with Mr. Shuttleworth in 1911 had in partial process of design. The matter was taken up with him, and as a result of the whole discussion with the Ontario Government and the officers of my own department and Mr. Moore we have entered into

an agreement with the Ontario Government to co-operate on some further peat experiments, 'building two types of peat machinery and operating them either at the same bog as before or some other bog, which matter is yet to be determined, each department of the Government, both federal and provincial, to bear equal proportions of the cost as to getting out designs, and the construction and installation of the machinery, for the purpose of seeing if we cannot once and for all solve the question as to whether peat can be handled in a cheap way in order to put it on the market if anthracite coal were to go down one or two dollars a ton from its present price. Unless we can do that, there is no stability or promise for development of peat manufacture on a very, very large scale. I would like to say frankly that anything that can be done this year cannot possibly do much to offset any possible fuel shortage next winter. Hon. gentlemen will understand that. But if we can get this machinery out in time to operate, or any information as to how to do it, even next year-'but I hope to do it this year-if we can get it out and show that we can produce peat by 'this sort of machinery at a price which will justify its development on a larger scale, we will have done enough to justify the expenditure of the time and money spent on this subject which, as the hon. member for Lambton has said', is of immense importance to the country.
Has the minister investigated the Graham process?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I know very little about Mr. Graham's process. I have heard of him as being a great enthusiast on the peat question. Some time ago he submitted certain suggestions and processes to the department, which were not thought at all practicable by the officials. I believe Mr. Graham dissents from, that view. Certainly, if he wishes to .submit any other processes we shall be only too glad to give them our consideration. I understand he wanted some substantial assistance in the way of development, but we did not intend to do anything more than what I have mentioned, because that is enough for this year.
I want to say in conclusion that I appreciate what my hon. friend from Lambton has said. I would like to say that, as a comparatively new Minister of Mines, I quite admit it has been unfortunate for the department that there have been so many ministerial changes, because I quite understand that such conditions do not promote

continuity of policy or of work or enthu&-iasm on the part of the officials'. But, so far as my knowledge goes, in that department there are a very large number of exceedingly able men, thoroughly well trained, enthusiastic, thoroughly keen about their work, and just as anxious to help their country in these war times as anybody else. Where the department is weak, it will be my duty to .strengthen it. If there are any mouldered branches they should certainly be lopped off. I shall bear in mind any criticism that the hon. member has made, and if, as a result of that, we can speed up our work, his resolution, as far as I am concerned, will not have been useless.

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the
motion carries I wish to make a few remarks, not wholly upon the motion but upon a .phase of the address of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong), and possibly of some of the addresses that followed. When I spoke on a similar subject on a motion by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) about a week ago, I did so merely as a substitute, called hastily to the task, for one of the other ministers, and speaking in that capacity I naturally did observe what I thought was a becoming reserve and, perhaps, hesitancy. What I shall say to-night will be entirely on that phase of the addresses that constituted something in the nature of an attack on the Mines Branch of the department over which I preside, and, consequently, I suppose I can speak with that freedom and clearness to which the House is always entitled. In order that hon. members may not have the question of responsibility confused, may I first of all draw this distinction: The Mines Department is a department under the ministry of the Secretary of State. As to that, I have, as a minister, nothing further to do than as a colleague. The Mines Branch of the Department of the Interior is an entirely different organization. That branch has to do with the administration of mining properties in so far as they belong to the Government of Canada^ that is to say, wherever mines are found on lands, the property of the Dominion, those mi.nes themselves are administered by the Mines Branch of the Department of the Interior. Consequently, Hudson bay lands, Canadian
Pacific lands, and all lands granted before a certain date some years ago, in regard to which lands the patent carried with it all the minerals and mines, are in no way under the Mines Branch of the Department of the Interior, and with them, of course, we have no concern. These lands having been alienated and being now private property, their administration as such comes wholly within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. The Mines Department is an entirely different institution from the Mines Branch. Not only is it a distinct entity, but its character and its purpose are wholly different. Its object, as I understand it, is the development and the fostering of the mining industry in this country, the encouragement and the help of that industry. The Branch of Mines under the Department of the Interior has to do with mines themselves in so far as they are the property of the Dominion. That being clear, first of all, hon. members will have no difficulty in determining what are the references to which it is my duty to reply.
It has been alleged by the hon. member for East Lambton, not on his own responsibility-for his courtesy I wish to give him full credit and thanks-but on the responsibility of others, including two officials of the Mines Department, that there was laxity in the administration of the Mines Branch of the Department of the Interior, resulting in a very serious waste of gas in mines in the province of Alberta under the control and administration of the department. In this connection, the hon. member read a letter from the Deputy Minister of the Mines Department. That the quotation may be fresh in the memory of the House, I will read the letter again:
Ottawa, January 8, 1918. Dear Mr. Armstrong:
Your letter of the 2nd instant to the Minister of Mines relative to the waste of natural gas in northern Alberta was referred to this offioe for attention.
I have consulted with Mr. D. B. Dowling of the Geological Survey, and from him I learn that the waste of gas is not nearly so large as you have been told.
There is, however, some waste both at Peace River and at other places in northern Alberta. At present the operators can practically do as they please, and it is high time that some regulations were formulated aiming at controlling their actions.
In addition to the waste of gas, there is also danger of faulty or careless boring injuring or destroying gas horizons by letting in water.
The great gas field in northern Alberta is under -the control of the Interior Department, and leases to bore for gas or oil are issued by them. I have already drawn their attention to the pressing need of regulations to govern

No.
Mr. ItlEIGHEN: At all events, there was such a committee, and I am told that in the whole six years of the last Parliament they met on only two or three occasions, so that unless the cohimittee were to attend more sedulously to its work, or unless it had more work to do than had the last Standing Committee on Mines, I do not see how they would accomplish very much towards bringing the Mines Branch to a sense of its obligations.
Mr. W. A. BUCHANAN (Lethbridge). The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) has made allusion to the existence of natural gas in northern Alberta and has dealt with the statements made by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong). I do not intend to make much reference to the natural gas resources of northern Alberta further than to say that in perhaps the most productive coal region of Alberta there is also a great quantity of natural gas, and that in the city of Medicine Hat practically all the fuel is natural gas; and the same may be said of the cities of Lethbridge and Calgary. In the city of Lethbridge there are also the greatest domestic coal mines of Alberta; so there is no doubt we have plenty of fuel resources in that part of Canada.
I feel it my duty to-night to allude to the coal resources, particularly of western Canada. I am not going to give any figures, but I would like to point out that there is no doubt that the mines in existence in western Canada at the present tiifie are capable of supplying all the needs of the western provinces, and undoubtedly they could supply some of the needs of eastern Canada. I am not quite sure, however, that it is feasible to ship western coal to the eastern market, because western coal up to the present time has been used wholly for the western market and it has not yet been established that it could be shipped and successfully compete with other coals in the eastern market. Its fuel quality is lost by storage and also by

transportation, and fjorn information I have I believe it would be a very costly coal by the time it reached Ontario. But I do feel this, that western coal could supply the market of western Canada and enable the eastern provinces to use a great amount of the coal that comes at the present time from Pennsylvania into the West. But difficulties are immediately met with. I do not know whether the members of this House realize that shipments of coal from Pennsylvania to western Canada have something to do with the rate on grain on the Great Lakes. The ships leave ports at the head of the lakes with grain from western Canada, but they want something to carry back, and at the present time they are carrying hack Pennsylvania coal at a very cheap rate. If they were unable to carry Pennsylvania coal it might mean an increase in the rate of grain going east along the Great Lakes; there is that fact to be considered in this matter. There is no question, however, that the coal resources of western Canada are quite capable of supplying the western Canada market. I have frequently seen in the constituency I represent a field of grain, and with it a coal mine-not a large mine, hut a mine that was supplying a good many farmers in that particular district.
We have mines of that character spread all through southern and Central Alberta, and I presume, also, through northern Alberta. Our western coal deposits start in Saskatchewan. We'have in Alberta the Lethbridge fields, the Drumheller fields, and the Crow's Nest fields, which are largely steam coal and coking coal. Then we have anthracite coal west of Calgary and west of Red Deer. There are also great deposits of coal in the Edmonton district and west of it. So that Alberta is particularly rich in its coal resources, and no province of western Canada is more capable of increasing production of coal than Alberta. I might point out that during this past season, when there was a demand for Pennsylvania coal for eastern Canada, there was a greater export of it into western Canada than the year previous.
I have had occasion before in this House to refer to the difficulty in connection with the operation of the mines regularly during these years. You are always going to have difficulties with labour, because labourers demand steady employment, which they do not secure in the mines of Alberta, -because the demand upon the mines of Alberta is made largely in the fall and winter months. The season slackens off in the early sDring and summer, and the mines are not work-

ed except on half or quarter time. Consequently hundreds of miners are out of employment during those months. If it were possible to store coal so that the mines could operate all through the year and store a supply of coal in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, it might be possible to operate the mines during the whole year, and provide steady employment for the miners, and I think the Government should direct its attention largely to this question of storage, because if it can solve that matter it will add a great deal to the production of coal the year round in Alberta. It is claimed that the coal produced in Alberta loses its fuel value when stored. But a number of propositions have been advanced which seem to me to be quite feasible, by which this can be overcome, and if it were overcome it would mean that the mines in that province could ship coal in the spring and summer months to large cities to the east of us and have it stored for use in the early winter; and this would enable them to keep up with the demand during the winter months. That is a matter to which I thiink the Government should pay considerable attention, and as there have been what appear to he very useful inventions made in connection with this matter of storing coal, I would suggest that the Government give the matter consideration. I have been discussing this question on several occasions in the House, and I do not know that I can say anything further. But I do not want the people of eastern Canada to run away with the idea that it is yet feasible to use western Canada coal in the eastern provinces. At the same time I would like to have that fact established, because the greater markets we have for our coal, not only in western Canada, but in eastern Canada, the greater would be the output from our mines, the more steady the employment of our miners, and the greater our wealth. But it is doubtful whether western Canada coal can be shipped to compete with Pennsylvania coal in the markets of eastern Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. DOUGLAS (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
speechtext:
I desire to congratulate
the mover of this resolution on bringing this very important subject to the attention of the House. I do not, however, desire to follow him in the various aspects of the subject with which the resolution deals, but more particularly to consider that portion of the resolution which reads:
That the deposits of bituminous and anthracite coal in Canada located in the extreme eastern and western portions thereof, be more

fully and thoroughly utilized for the benefit of the residents of the central provinces.
I take it that, in that connection, the most important, or at least one of the most important, duties that to-day devolves upon the Government is in regard to the increase in the production of coal within our own country. If there are three things most important for us I submit, they are the question of the supply of men, the supply of food, and the supply of fuel; and it is difficult to put any one of these propositions as first ahead of the others. But it is to the production of coal, particularly in eastern Canada, that I wish, for the time being, to direct the attention of the House. It is said that Canada consumes about thirty million tons of coal annually. Approximately one-half of this is produced in this country, and of that production of coal in Canada approximately one-half is produced in the far western part of the country, and the other part, approximately seven million tons, is produced in the extreme eastern part of Canada. Coal production in eastern Canada is confined almost exclusively to the counties of Pictou, Cumberland. Inverness and Cape Breton. Further analyzing it, it is confined, in a large measure, to one single cofinty in eastern Canada, namely, Cape Breton. It becomes particularly pertinent to inquire at this time whether or not everything is being done that ought to he done by the fuel administration and the Government to secure increased production of coal in eastern Canada. What I desire to submit for the consideration of the House is this: if the fuel controller, with his manifold duties, is charged only with the responsibility of borrowing coal from the United States, I would be inclined to think that, perhaps, he has not been entirely unsuccessful in his efforts; but if, as I take it, the prime duty of the fuel controller is to see that we in Canada produce our quota of coal and of fuel, then I say that, as far as eastern Nova Scotia is concerned, the fuel controller has not measured up to the occasion and to the conditions as they obtain. The facts are these: since 1913 the coal production in Nova Scotia has been gradually but surely diminishing. The coal sales in Nova Scotia for the five years past have been as follows:

cial fiscal year of 1918, we find that the decreased production of bituminous coal in eastern Canada in comparison with the previous year will reach 600,000 tons. There has been a decrease in the production of coal in eastern Canada since the war broke out of upwards of 2,000,000 tons. Since the fuel controller took office in July of last year, there has been a decrease in production of 600,000 tons, and there is the estimate of a further reduction in output of 600.000 tons in 1918. Viewed from the standpoint of increased production-and that is one of the greatest questions that we should he dealing with at- the present time-the fuel controller and the administration, in regard [DOT]to fuel, have not been entirely successful. The decrease in output, in five years, amounted to 1,400,000 tons, and adding this to the decrease that is expected by the operators and the Mines Department in Nova Scotia this year, the total will exceed 2,000,000 tons.
The great question then, that we have to deal with in this connection is how we can increase the coal output in eastern Canada. This subject naturally divides itself under two heads: (1) Increase in the production of the mines now producing coal, and (2) the reopening of collieries not now producing coal. The collieries now operating might be made to produce a very considerable quantity of coal over that which is now being produced. You may a-sk me what is the reason why the Nova Scotia mines are not keeping up to their normal output. The reasons are well known, I am sure, to some hon. gentlemen here. I would say, that (1) production could be increased by compelling the coal companies and operators to more equitably deal with the employees under them; (2) by increasing the wages of certain classes of labour, particularly the underpaid men who are working in the collieries; and (3) by reducing the large overhead charges to which most of these companies are subject. I have one instance in mind of a company that produces 500,000 tons of coal and pays to its general manager a salary of $100,000. In other words, for every ton



of coal produced by thi3 company, the general manager receives twenty cents. Or, to put it in another' way: this company does not market all its output; it consumes
400.000 tons itself; it has a little less than
100.000 tons of coal to be sold in the markets, and its general manager receives as salary one dollar for every ton of coal produced by this company and sold in the market. Can you wonder that, under these conditions, there should be such unrest as has characterized the coal mine operations in eastern Canada for the last few years and particularly for the past few months?
I further submit as a suggestion that improved mining machinery should be brought into the various operating mines in Nova Scotia. Some of the coal companies are making exhorbitant profits while some of them are merely getting along under present conditions. I submit as a principle, these being war-time profits, that the companies that are making profits should be obliged to put back into the operation of their collieries by improved development and by improved mining machinery the amounts that they have received in excess of what would be normal profits under normal conditions. More encouragement should be given to the miners in the line of production and instructions whereby they might be made more competent to carry on the several operations in connection with mining.
It may be said by hon. gentlemen, as it is said by operators, that one of the prime difficulties encountered is the shortage of labour. 'It is true that there is a shortage of labour for mining operations, but tha't is not the only reason why there has been such a decrease in production. I submit that in the course of the three and one-half years during which we have been at war there should have been ample time for the making of miners. You can train men to work on the farm, and it is not any more difficult to make competent and skilful miners although it may take a little longer time. Nevertheless, there is a shortage of skilled miners that- might 'be offset by the fact that we have men of good physique growing up in the various occupations connected with mining who are capable of producing coal, running machines and performing the other operations in connection with mining. A man with a coal-mining machine can produce as much as 52 tons of coal a day. A hand-pick miner gets out a very few tons of coal per day in proportion. Why should there not be more mining machines introduced into the mines of Nova Scotia? As far as trans-

portation is concerned, why should the companies not be obliged to have box car loading apparatus? I am told that one of the difficulties in connection with the shipment of coal is that connected with transportation. The mining companies say that they are unable to get coal cars and consequently are obliged to. load their product into the box cars that are supplied by the railways. A small expenditure for the equipment of box car loaders would reduce the cost Of fuel by from twenty-five cents to thirty cents per ton. The goal companies should modernize themselves and get improved machinery with the profits they are getting which are largely war-time profits. It is the duty of the Government and of the fuel controller to see that increased production is brought about in the mines of -Nova Scotia.
What is needed in this country is a speeder-up. Just as they have in certain portions of the mining sections in England a speeder-up they ought to have a speeder-up here, a man with broad powers who is able to see that regulations, properly fiamed, are carried Out with a view to increased production.
"When you consider that the normal production of coal in Nova Scotia increased^at the rate of ten per cent every year for the last fifty to one hundred years, and that only when war broke out the collieries of that province did not even maintain their usual output but went behind to the extent of at least ten per cent per annum, I venture to say that if a speeder-up, with power such as I have suggested, is placed in charge of the situation in Nova Scotia, he will bring back its coal production tp the normal figure. He will not only do that, but he will gradually restore the increase of ten per cent which was witnessed for many years anterior to the war. I make that suggestion to the House, and I trust that the Government and the fuel controller's department, which is charged particularly with the responsibility of increasing the production of fuel, will give their best consideration to it.
Not only has speeding up been successful in England, but it has met with equally gratifying results in the province of Alberta. Owing to labour difficulties, Mr. Armstrong was placed in charge of the operations in one of the coal sections of Alberta, and what has been the result? I understand that there has been a great increased production in that section of the country. Bearing in mind the results obtained in England and Alberta, and with _ the prevailing situation in Nova Scotia, where

there are two million tons less coal produced to-day than before the war broke out, it becomes a pertinent matter that the Government should be properly advised, and it becomes their paramount duty to consider the appointment of a satisfactory man to speed up production in that part of Canada. Not only does that apply to the mines now operating, but there is also a situation to be met with respect to the mines that are not producing coal. These collieries might probably be divided into two classes:	first, the collieries that
closed down before the war broke out, and second, the collieries that closed down owing to the war panic and to other reasons. Take the former class, and I submit that with proper encouragement they could be made producing collieries within a very short time. Let me give you one instance in support of that statement. The Greenwood Coal Company, incorporated with a capital of $50,000, last year produced forty thousand tons of coal as a result of the Nova Scotia Government advancing them the sum of $25,000 to open their property. Within two years they have been able to refund the amount so advanced by the local Government with interest, and last year, as I say, they obtained an output of forty thousand tons. I think that this year, with the daily output now exceeding three hundred tons, they ought to produce tor the twelve months ninety to one hundred thousand tons of coal. The same policy if applied to other companies should be followed by equally gratifying results.
It may toe said, what has this to do with the matter of increasing coal production or the re-opening of coal mines? Under normal conditions, I admit, it is properly the duty of the provinces to deal with matters pertaining to mines, and particularly to coal; but when we are dealing with war conditions, I submit, as a reasonable proposition which will be accepted by the House, that it becomes the duty of the Federal Government to develop a proper policy for the increased production of fuel. I could give many specific instances where increased production would be Obtained; where in one case one hundred thousand tons of coal would Ibe secured within twelve months, and in other cases lesser amounts. Suffice it to say that in the counties of Cape Breton and Inverness there are collieries not now in operation that could be made, within a year, to produce from three to four hundred thousand tons. So that I say
49i
there are two problems facing the fuel 'administration:	one is 'to increase the
production of the mines now operating, and the other is to put the mines that are not operating into a condition where they may 'be made to produce; and I think I am not over-istating the matter wdien I suggest to the fuel controller and his department that a man, almost an autocrat in the powers conferred upon him, should be appointed to take hold of the *coal situation in eastern Canada-a man with power to make advances, to take over and operate collieries, to have supervision of methods of mining and so on. These suggestions, Mr. Speaker, I have made having in view increased production which I regard as one of the great essentials in connection with the w-ar administration at the present time. I have not attempted to deal with the general subject, and perhaps my remarks have been largely of a local nature; but they have to be largely of a local nature, in view of the fact that one third of the coal that is produced in Canada is produced locally- practically in the town in which I live. So that if there is a local aspect to my treatment of the subject it is due merely to that fact; but on the broad, national question of increased production, I submit, the Government and the fuel administration should see to it that increased production is obtained by the appointment of an energetic man with large and broad powers, in order to ensure that in 1918 our output will be gTeatly increased over that of the past year.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. H. HALLADAY (Bow River, Alta.):
speechtext:
I had hoped that when the hon. minister at the head of the department having control of this subject was speaking this afternoon he would mention coal in some way in his discourse. He took up the gas and pulp question, but I failed to hear the word coal mentioned in his speech. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan), when he says that Alberta is quite capable of furnishing western Canada with all the coal it requires; and this can be done without opening up a new mine or increasing the capacity of the present mines. The hon. member who introduced this motion gave us figures this afternoon of coal production in Alberta which are quite correct. We can produce in that province with the mines we have at present, twice .as much if not three times as much with one extra shift. The scarcity of coal is not the fault of the mines, but is due to lack of transportation, as. far as the Red Deer valley is concerned. We say that

during the last three weeks we have been unable to get trains from Calgary to Drumheller, the spot where the Red Deer Valley coal mines are. This railroad has been operating some five years and every spring it has been held up from one to three weeks. They have not had a train over that railroad for three weeks on account of twenty small bridges (being washed out. In conversation with the coal operators at Drumheller a short time ago, they advised me that with the present shift they could double their output if the Canadian Northern Railway would furnish the oars. They also said that if they were able to secure mine-operating machinery, such as box car loaders and diamond cutters, I believe they called them, they could double their output with the same number of men. It is not a question of opening up mines, but of being able to operate the mines we have and ship the coal. I would like to call the attention of the ministers to the fact that the operators need this coal-mining machinery, which is not manufactured in Canada. If some inducement could be offered to these people they would be able to purchase this machinery, but at the present high rate of duty they claim that they are unable to do so. I would go further: if they are unable to purchase this machinery, even with the duty off, it would be good business for the Government to purchase that machinery, sell it to the operators, and take payment in the shape of royalties. Coal is going to be needed. 1 understand that England shipped over to the port of New York some time last fall two shiploads of coal in order to coal vessels which were waiting to take back munitions. Now, if by taking the duty off this coal-mining machinery, or even by purchasing it to be installed in our western mines, and so bringing about the desired effect, I would very much favour that course.

Mr. Speaker, I have been for nearly ten years in the Chamber, a colleague of my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) who introduced this resolution, and gave one of the ablest speeches, so far as form and delivery are concerned, that I have heard from him. I have listened to him frequently with pleasure, and have always admired his activity, energy and attention to detail, but I have scarcely ever been able to agree with his conclusions; and the resolution of to-day is no exception to what has been the unfortunate experience of the past. I sincerely and profoundly wish that my hon. friend, with his great ability, would
[(Mr. Halhiday ]
devote himself to the study of economics fundamentally and I am quite sure that I should soon have a very powerful colleague in the advocacy of free trade in this House.
Having for years endeavoured, with indifferent success, to carry economic light into the dark places of the other side of the House, I am not unwilling to make a slight attempt to explore the country which may be more thick and more difficult still. Mr. Speaker, a resolution like this and a debate like this on general principles are only possible in a protectionist country. The problem which seemed to engage the minds of the introducer of the motion and of my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan) who followed him, was the problem of scarcity in the midst of abundance. And when one comes to think of it, Sir, it is a problem. We have enough coal in Canada, I heard some one say during the reciprocity debates-to last the world two thousand years. Perhaps that was a slight exaggeration. In those same debates I used to say that if that was the case we need not bother much about certain of the arguments against reciprocity, because, unless protectionists mended their ways, they would be getting their fuel cheap enough long before that time. With all that coal, Sir, in the earth, we nevertheless have had circumstances during the past winter in which the people have been strained to death to get coal to keep themselves warm, in a climate that frequently goes to forty below zero. Well, now, Sir, that is a problem. And it strikes me that thoughtful men, approaching that problem with an open mind, would at once see that there is something radically wrong with the economic thought of the people of the country, and that is exactly my theory about what is wrong. My hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Douglas) has just told us that we have the melancholy spectacle in Nova Scotia of the amount of coal produced declining from year to year. There was a fine old member of this House, Mr. Carmichael, who enjoyed in an eminent degree the friendship of the right hon the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and he objected to a duty being put on coal and lost his seat for it in the province of Nova Scotia. Well, he wtould have had a better chance to keep his seat in western Canada, we have more enlightened people economically there. Personally, I prefer the heresy-if it was a heresy-of Mr. Carmichael to the present motion. You have, according to my hon. friend from Cape Breton, decreased production under a tariff. And yet we have a proposal brought before the House here

to-day that another form of protection should be applied in the shape of what is practically a bounty. The tariff has decreased the production-no getting away from that fact; we have just heard it stated by *a man who knows. You say: we cannot do it by tariff; let us give them some money to do it. Well, I daresay that any industry would be the better of any money you gave it, but my friend who advocates that, in what was a very able speech from his point of view-if you do not pay too much attention to what he said-also told us that it is more important to produce food even than fuel at this time. If I put it to him as tto what he would say to me if, representing the western constituencies, I came here to-night and said: Let the Government go into mining wheat on a' large scale we need food more than fuel-he would say: That is absurd, we are producing the wheat anyway. That is exactly the proper answer. If you will allow capital to take its own bourse under freedom you will produce, and produce all that your capital is capable of producing, by giving them markets in which to sell. There is no subject in the world on which there is so much confused thinking as on this question of protection and free trade. I remember during the reciprocity debates that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) in a very long speech, a speech of four hours duration-
Oh, my!

-objected to reciprocity on one particular ground, and that was that the United States would exhaust the resources of Canada-our raw material would all be sent over to the United States. The other side of the confused thinking is that hon. gentlemen come to this House to-day, and they get into an awful state about a little bit of coal finding its way from Pennsylvania to Saskatchewan So that they on their part object to exhausting the resources of the United States. I am so good a patriot and so much a believer in cheap coal that I would say: Take the duty off coal altogether and get all your coal from the United States, and then you will conserve the (Canadian product for future generations'. You will keep all our coal; you will be all that to the good. You will get cheap coal from the United States. You will exhaust the United States supply, and then you will have all this 2,000 years' supply left. My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan), defending himself needlessly in a very able speech against the charge of being parochial, said that he would desire to approach this subject not only from the local point of view, the provincial point of view, but as a Dominion-wide subject. Well, I thought to myself, my hon. Mend is very near the kingdom; he needs to take just another step and he will become a bigger man than his thought, and his programme will be a better one. He wants to make hi.s creed world-wide, and1 then he will become a free trader.
A tariff is, inevitably, an artificial restriction of .production. We have had the results stated to-night, so that we have to give a bounty as well as have a tariff. What is the real promoter of production? Trade is the real promoter of production. People produce only what they can sell, if they are right in the top story. You cannot promote production by artificial means. Not only is trade the real promoter of production, it is the only promoter of wealth. We sometimes, and indeed, we continually hear at the present time of production a6 if it were an. end in itself. Production is not an end in itself, and it is not even the source of wrealth. Trade is the source of wealth and the only source o,f the development- of great wealth. Let me give the House an example. A few years ago we produced in this country 300,000,000 bushels of wheat in one year. We use in this country only 60,000,000 bushels of wheat in- one year. Clearly, the 240,000,000 bushels of excess product over what we were able to use. that year in this country was not wealth until we could send it abroad and exchange it. It is only by being able to exchange it or trade it for something else that it becomes wealth. You have a still more striking illustration of that in Australia at the present moment. You have the product-wheat-of two years' crop stored in bags, and owing to the difficulties of transportation it cannot be exchanged, with the result that it is growing musty and rotting, and being wasted from the bags by rodents which are having access to it. It is so far from being wealth that it is an incumbrance in the hands of the people. Trade is the real promoter of production and the real and only promoter of wealth. I do not know, but I would suggest that the reason why they are not mining that coal in Saskatchewan, about which the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) has told us, is that they found it more profitable to mine wheat there. You do not need to give them money to make them wheat miners there. The market and the supply make them mine the wheat. It is possible in this connection to reduce tba protectionist theory to an absolute absurdity.
Does the hon. gentleman not believe in any such thing as control, food control, for instance?

I believe in control of my speech when I have not something wise to say. I was saying, Sir, that it is possible to reduce to an absurdity the theory of protection that was advanced in this debate, by inference, if not by absolute statement. Hon. gentlemen who have spoken in support of this resolution have, all of them, gone on the theory that we should, if possible, produce in Canada all the coal we need. We do produce in Canada all the wheat we need. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. .Cockshutt) would certainly believe in producing in Canada all the agricultural implements we need, and the protectionist, who has any other goods to peddle, would believe in producing in Canada all of anything that we can use. But in that case, if it were possible to succeed, you would have a huge excess of all your products. Under the protectionist theory, what would you do with your excesses? The thing is so absurd on the face of it that I do not yet despair before I die of getting some light into this House. It is hard work, but I do not despair.
This is a serious, practical question for the people of this country at the present time, and while I am, as everybody knows, in favour of producing all we can for the conduct of the war, I do not want, to go about the matter in a senseless fashion. I think my hon. friend suggested that free mining implements would be a good thing in this country. We are very slow in this country. In the Argentine Republic they have not had a duty on mining tools for years, or if they have a duty at all, it is merely a nominal one. Just imagine the wisdom of people who think they will mine coal more easily if they make dear the implements with which they do their mining. I would sayHave a trial of freedom along the line of mining implements, if the question of production toe so important. There is the road to production. I pointed it out the other day in connection with food. The first step in increasing the production of food is to have free agricultural implements. I point it out again now, quoting the example of the Argentine Republic in connection with coal. Free the implements with which you produce coal; take off all the restrictions, but do not try to increase the production of coal by giving money away where the tariff has failed. The giving of money for the specific purpose of building up any

specific industry toy way of bounty, or whatever you call it, would, with the present demands on the public purse, be little short of an economic crime.
With regard to the coal question, I want to put in a word for the consumer. The protectionist is always looking to the producer. The only sound way of looking at this economic question is always to look to the consumer, because w'e are all consumers. We consume one hundred things where we only produce one, and if you look to the consumer and let capital take its free course, it will always find the line of least resistance. You will produce most in that way of all that your country is capable of producing, compatibly with marketing the produce.
At the .present juncture, I am looking at this from the point of view of the consumer, and if one goes into the houses of Ottawa and talks to the rank and file of the common people, one finds that the hardships of the war are coming very close to them in this matter of fuel. I cannot imagine any more insensate folly than to keep a duty on coal in a country like this, where the temperature goes down to forty and fifty below zero, and where the people in the capital city last year bad to suffer almost privation for the want of material to. keep themselves warm; I cannot imagine anything more absurd. The geographical position- of the two countries makes it an ideal case for no tariff. You have an imaginary boundary line between the United States and Canada of 3.000 miles. At one part of the boundary line you have coal to the south and you have not coal to the north, and at another part of the boundary line you have coal to the north and not coal to the south. Could anything be more foolish than to prevent the exchange across the line, and to endeavour to keep carrying the long distances in both the countries concerned? I cannot imagine anything more foolish under the sun, I repeat, than keeping a duty on coal at the present juncture.
Our people are beginning to feel the burden of the war. Why increase it to them? We are looking forward to a winter in which the privations of the people of Ottawa may be greater than they were last year. I recommend to the House that instead of giving away money along the old sweet path for the artifician promotion of any industry whatsoever, we should try first the simpler plan. One remembers in this connection the lines:
Oh, -how unlike the complex works of man, Heaven's easy, artless, unencumbered plan!

Free your implements. Free your coal; let it go across the border. The difficulties of the war, of course, enter into one's consideration ; we cannot alter them; they are with us. But we can help them out, and if I wanted to make sure, so far as I can see into this question, that I was going to make it easier for the consumers of coal in this country next winter than it was last winter I would say, take the duty off coal altogether, and let them go at this coal in the United States, and keep our own for future generations if capital ha's not found it profitable up to date to mine it.

Might I say in a brief and somewhat pre-sumptous reply-if I may call it so to my hon. friend from Red Deer, that he has proceeded on an entirely false -assumption which utterly and absolutely invalidates his. argument. If this world were composed of one nation; if the people were identical in their interests; if the different nations that exist at the present time were only different states of the same union his argument would undoubtedly be sound. But we are up against this fact: there exists in the world a certain human failing or weakness which is called business rivalry, and it is only necessary in order to prove my point to call the hon. gentleman's attention to one fact, and that is the death of agriculture in England. If Great Britain had properly protected her agriculture, and had not pursued the policy which the hon. gentleman has enunciated she would not be in the desperate position she is in today as regards food.
While Germany is well off.

She would be in the
position of having developed and maintained a certain national industry, so that it would make no difference to her whether there was a German submarine policy or not, or whether Canada w.as in existence or not. But heretofore -she has proceeded on the assumption of my hon. friend, and endeavoured to feed the world on her manu-facture-s. You cannot live on Sheffield cutlery or on Manchester cotton goods, and the consequence was that when war came, the hon. gentleman's policy found that good old country in the desperate condition in regard to- food that she is in to-day. Had it n-ot been for that policy England would now be in a better position. It is one of the greatest possible c-a>ta-strophies that such a policy as my hon, friend has just enunciated has heretofore obtained in England.
My hon. friend -must be -a mathematician. He labours under the impression that free trade or trade policies are like the principle of the conservation of energy, that where something manifests itself there must be a compensation also, that there is a transformation but never a dissipation of energy. Now, that is not the case with regard to trade. Trade and the principles of trade can easily be suppressed, and the patent law alone ought to show him that the protection exercised by means of that law would itself dislocate all trade. You cannot lay down any such principles as he has laid down so long as you have national boundaries, so long ae there is one country up against another, so long as you have a number of countries in close rivalry one with another. Sweep away these boundaries, make humanity one, and what he says is true, provided that you can correct that other weakness of humanity, native greed. If only people will be considerate of each other, if only the Turks will spare the Armenians; if only the Armenians when they send up their prayers to -Heaven are considered -by the Almighty worthy of being spared and are spared- but the trouble is, when they send up their prayers to Heaven, month after month and year after year, the Almighty turns a deaf ear to -them, and Canada and the United States and every other country are asked to subscribe for their protection. Why, you ask at once, should we subscribe for their protection when the Almighty himself refuses to protect them? We must proceed to the -bottom of this thing, we must investigate the fundamental principles, and the one fundamental principle is this, that so long as there is this national rivalry throughout the world an easy natural -adjustment such as my hon. friend has referred to is altogether and absolutely out of the question.

I had not intended to intervene in this debate, but I cannot allow to pass unchallenged the economic fallacies which I have heard enunciated by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burnham). He first of all says that Great Britain in this war has been suffering from her free trade policy. Let me ask him this:	Are the people of Germany or of
Austria better fed to-day than are the people of England? I do not think so, unless our newspapers are leading us astray by wrong information. Let us review for a few brief moments the history of free trade in Great Britain.
Order	.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to restrict his remarks upon the free trade policy of Great Britain, to what application it may have to the motion before the House.

The question of coal is before the House. Surely, Mr. Speaker, as a preliminary observation, I can set the hon. gentleman right as to the economic principles, or rather the fallacies and the heresies which he has enunciated.
Just as an observation.

By way of observation. We have in Quebec notarial deeds, and those deeds sometimes start out with what are called preliminary observations, and mine will be a preliminary observation. Before they had free trade in England the people were starving, and the question before the British people for the first half of the nineteenth century was whether the population of Great Britain and Ireland would emigrate, or whether they would allow free foods to come in from abroad to feed the people at home, in exchange for the coal and manufactures of Great Britain. Hon. gentlemen will see that I have not departed far from the subject. It is quite true, as the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) says, that you cannot live off Sheffield cutlery. No, but you can exchange it for flour from the United States or Canada, and live on the flour. The British people were starving before they had free trade in England. The people of Great Britain had to have free interchange of foodstuffs for their coal and other articles before they could live. I desire to point out that Great Britain, through her policy of free trade in coal and other things, has been able, not only to finance herself, but, at the beginning of the war to finance the overseas dominions, including Canada, and also very largely her Allies. I think if there were anything required to show the*sound principle of the fiscal policy of the Old Country, it was the way she was able to stand the terrible financial strain caused by the war. I would not like to think that all economic truths had to be administered to this Government by the back door. I should like to show them that there are economic principles to be enunciated which they must meet face to face.

As coal
production is the burning question to-night, and as I come from a coal producing county, I desire to make a few observations with
[ IM r. MciMa s te r. ]
regard to coal production in the county of Pictou, which I represent. With regard to the price of coal as arranged by the fuel controller or his agents, I understand the prices for the Acadia Coal Company are $6.60 for screened coal, $6.35 for run of mine and $5.25 for culm. If a measure-able proportion of this unreasonable increase went into the pockets of the mine workers, I would1 not complain and I believe the people would not complain. In discussing this matter with the accountant, who I understand went to Nova Scotia to investigate the cost of production at the different collieries, he gave the information that, in arriving at a price for the Acadia Coal Company, he estimated $100,000 for repairs or development work for the Allan Shaft mine, and $30,000 for another mine. The company to be reimbursed for said amount in three years. Also that he took into account the capitalization of the company which, I understand, to be five millions; that is three millions of preferred stock and two millions of common. In addition to this he has, no doubt, taken into account the large and highly paid official management of the company, which means very large overhead expense.	I
wish to object to the	method of
book-keeping as adopted by this expert. In the first place, the public, in my opinion, should not be called upon to reimburse the company to the extent of $130,000, or to pay dividends on the company's mistakes, or to pay__ dividends on millions of watered stock. Neither should they be called upon to pay excessive salaries to the management. It must be understood that the Acadia Coal Company are now producing only about 600 t-ons of coal per day, whereas, the official management is big enough for a company that could take care of the production of 6,000 tons per day. Taking the argument of this accountant, and figuring the cost of production on a basis of 600 tons per day, he has decided that the company should be paid $6.60 per ton for screened coal, $6.35 for run of mine, and $5.25 for culm coal. Following his methods and his contention, if the company further reduced their output to 300 tons per day, and closed down another mine, I presume he would fix the price at $13j20 per ton for screened coal, $12.70 for run of mine, and $10.50 for culm. One trouble with the Acadia Coal Company is that they have closed down two collieries; another is that their overhead expense is entirely too great, and entirely out of proportion to their production. Within the past three months from 300 to 400 mine workers have left the town of Stellar-

ton because they could not obtain employment. It is true they have had trouble in the mines they are now operating. In the recent explosion which took place at the Allan shafts 88 precious lives were lost. I believe the county of Pictou sustained a greater actual loss of life in this explosion than the county has suffered in this great war up to the present time. A large number of widows and children are left homeless and penniless, and no investigation has taken place up to the present time, except a coroner's inquest, conducted by an aged medical doctor, assisted by two lawyers who are favourable to the company. In my opinion there should at once be a thorough investigation of all their mining properties by mining engineers of the first class. I have no desire to cause any injustice to be done to any of the coal mining companies in the county of Pictou; it is my duty to see that fair consideration is given to the coal companies, but consumers must be protected.	,
I know it is necessary for the companies to receive a fair increase in the price of coal, but I wish to protest in the strongest possible manner against the price of coal as arranged by the fuel controller for the Acadia Coal Company. The solution of the situation in so far as the Acadia Coal Company are concerned is for them to produce more coal and increase their output. They hold a blanket lease of large and valuable mine areas which they will neither operate nor permit others to operate. I suggest that this Government should co-operate with the local government, and take over the extensive leases held by the Acadia Coal Company and appoint a commission to operate the mines for the benefit of the public, or hand the said leases over to firms who are competent and willing to operate such leases and produce coal at a fair and reasonable price. If the company is permitted to impose the present prices that are in my opinion entirely unjustiable, it will mean serious hardship to the people of the Maritime Provinces, and especially to the people of the county I have the honour to represent. Such increase, if authorized, will embarrass the manufacturers and discourage further industrial development. I understand the Minister of Railways and Canals has fixed the price to be paid by his department for the coal required for railway purposes. The people will expect this Government to protect their interests and arrange that the prices to be paid by the manufacturers, the dealers, and the public shall be in keeping with the price paid by the Government for their requirements.
Mr. J. W. EDWARD'S (Frontenac): I listened with the usual pleasure and interest to the remarks of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and while I cannot agree with his point of view on trade matters, I am free to confess that the hon. gentleman is not only persistent in advocating his free trade principles, but he is also consistent in advocating them, and no person doubts his thorough sincerity in holding the views which he does hold. I am precluded from going into the question of free trade, I understand, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to trespass upon your goodi nature in that regard. I may say, however, that it does strike me that in a country such as we have in Canada we must, in framing our tariff policy, whether in regard to coal or anything else, take into consideration our climatic conditions as compared with those of other countries with which Canada has to compete. I will not attempt to follow that up any farther, but what I rose to say in regard to the coal question was this: The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) said that last winter there were actually people in the capital city of Ottawa who were suffering from cold on account of a shortage of coal, and that he regarded it as the height of absurdity to have a duty on coal when people were suffering from a shortage of coal. He said that when at one part of the continent north of the boundary line there was coal and none south of it, and when at another part there was coal south of the line and none north of it, it was, under such conditions, absurd to have a duty on coal. As I understand it, there is no duty on the coal that the people use in their furnaces and in their stoves. Anthracite coal passes freely from the other side of the line into Canada without any duty. The duty is only on bituminous coal. The tariff is as follows:
Coal, bituminous, slack, such as 95 per cent will pass through a three-quarter inch screen, per ton, 10c; 12e; 14c.
These rates being the British preferential tariff, the intermediate tariff and the general tariff. Item 588:
Coal, bituminous, round and run of mine, and coal, n.o.p. per ton, 35c; 45c; 53c.
These are not classes of coal that are used toy people in warming their houses.

I do not want
to make an unnecessary interruption, but I may say to my bon. friend that I am using a grate fire myself-the mornings are cold enough-and I am using tooth kinds of coal.

That may be true, but the hon. gentleman does not dispute my statement that in so far as his argument applies to people who are using coal for heating purposes in their houses, it falls down in that there is no duty on that class of coal. We did have trouble in this country last winter, but 'according to my idea it was due to the fact that there was a shortage of ears, that the United States had some 25,000 cars which should have been in Canada-they had that many more of our cars than we had of theirs. The great difficulty in obtaining coal for heating houses lay in the fact of the shortage of cars, the extreme winter and the days of blockade upon the railways on account of snow. I have no objection whatever to the hon. member for Red Deer holding views on trade matters. I give him credit for being perfectly sincere in his views. He is, at all events, always consistent. He is an out-and-out free trader, and he wants to see free trade in everything. That is a consistent view for him to take. He may hold that view if he chooses, but I do not think his argument was quite correct in so far as coal was concerned, because it left the impression that it was the duty on coal generally used by the people that was responsible, whereas there is no duty on that class of coal.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take very many minutes of the time of this House, but having listened to the hon. members from Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan and Alberta telling us what vast bodies of coal they have in those different provinces, I feel that I should tell the House that in British Columbia we have vast coal beds. Our climate is such that we do not require to burn so much coal as they do in Ontario, Quebec and some of the western provinces. If the people of these provinces have not sufficient coal next winter I would invite them to co-me to the Pacific coast, because we will have sufficient, heat to keep them quite warm. We have vast coal areas on Vancouver island, and besides supplying the lower mainland of British Columbia with coal, we ship as far south as San Francisco from 1,500,000 tons to 2,000,000 tons per year. You see, therefore, that we are not short of coal. The only thing we complain about is that the fuel controller does not keep down the price of coal to what it should be. In the city of Vancouver we pay $9 a ton for coal, and they only have to ship it forty miles across from Nanaimo. I think that is a question that

the fuel controller should look into and compel the mine owners to sell their coal at a less rate than they are charging. We have coal beds in the Nicola valley but we cannot ship our coal out from there because it costs too much to transport it to the larger centres of the province. We have coal in the Crow's Nest Pass from which they ship east. We have anthracite in northern British Columbia, in the Skeena river region. An American engineer has reported that there is almost ten times as much anthracite coal in the Skeena district as there is all kinds of coal in the whole province of Nova Scotia. I only wanted to inform the House that British Columbia is on the map when it comes to the question of coal.

Before mentioning the question of coal, I want to refer to one or two observations that were made by the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). I would not have said anything in regard to his argument were it not for the slap that he gave to Great Britain. I think it is very unbecoming, to say the least, for any hon. gentleman in this House to abuse Great Britain at this particular time for the purpose of bolstering up the protectionist argument. It only goes to show that the protectionist is now, as he always has been, prepared to slap his very best friend at any time to bolster up his own argument in any way in which it can be done. If he had only taken the trouble to analyse the quantity of food that Great Britain had control of and disposed of since this war began, he would not have used the argument which he did use to-night. We all know what Great Britain has done in the matter of feeding her Allies, we all know what she did for years until the United States took over the feeding of Belgium, and we all know what she has done more recently in regard to Italy, and I think it ill becomes the hon. gentleman to use that kind of argument. He himself states that we should go to the bottom of this argument. The present is not the time for that, Mr. Speaker, but I only hope that opportunity will be afforded to us before the session closes of going to the bottom of the trade argument with the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). We will be very glad to do it if the opportunity is presented, and we will try very hard to kick the bottom clean out.
Coming to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), we all know his tendencies. I might not go as far as he would go in

the matter of free trade, but I will say this: I will trade with anybody that will trade with me anything from a jack knife, to as far as you like to go, across the international boundary or anywhere else. It makes no difference to me what it is; if it is business I am prepared to do it. But I think the hon. gentleman has misinterpreted the meaning of the words that the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) may have used, although personally I did not hear what that hon. gentleman said this afternoon. I may say this, however: People in Saskatchewan, eastern Saskatchewan particularly, are probably somewhat differently situated from the residents of Alberta. We have the long freight haul; the freight on the coal in eastern Saskatchewan amounts to practically as much per ton as the coal costs at the mine. We have, as has been stated, an abundance of lignite coal which when briquetted, we are given to understand, is quite equal in. heating qualities to Pennsylvania coal. I understand the argument has been advanced that we should produce all our own coal within our own boundaries. I quite agree with that argument, providing it can be produced in an economical way. But in the province of 'Saskatchewan that cannot be done at the present time. It is true that we have anthracite coal in western 'Canada, and our friends in Alberta claim it is equally as good1 as Pennsylvania anthracite. That is a matter of opinion. Personally T like Pennsylvania anthracite when I can get it; but thiat is neither here nor there. The available quantities of coal of that particular quality in Alberta cannot be produced in large enough quantities to meet the demands in the province for that class of coal. We have got to have anthracite coal there in the winter time. If we did not have Pennsylvania anthracite coal at this particular time we would have to consign to the scrap heap -our base-burner coal stoves that can only be used satisfactorily with anthracite, or similar type of coal. Briquettes, if we had them, would work very satisfactorily, and that is the argument advanced foy the hon. member for Regina this afternoon. I understand, not that there should be a bounty, not that there should be protection, but that there should be an experiment as it were, or a demonstration that the use of this lignite is commercially and economically feasible. We have been working along that line for some considerable time, but is is largely private capital that has been used and it has been an uphill job.
What is now asked is that the Government should undertake to give a demonstration on a commercial scale to show that that coal can be produced economically. We are given to understand that with proper equipment this coal can be produced at almost one-half of what we have to pay for the Pennsylvania anthracite, and that the two coals are about equal in burning qualities.
In regard to the fuel controller's restrictions I would like to say that, while 1 have not had it direct from the controller's office, press reports give us to understand that restrictions are to be placed on the amount of coal that the consumer may store at one time. I do not know whether such restriction is intended to apply to western 'Canada, but if it is, the fuel controller will have made one of the most serious mistakes that any man placed in charge of fuel, or anything else in Canada, has so far committed. I hope that the fuel controller does not intend' to go that far. We in western Canada have got-and we have been educating our people to carry out this, policy-to put in our winter supply of soft coal during the summer months. The statement is made that coal deteriorates in storage. There are some kinds that will not deteriorate to any appreciable extent in storage. There are large quantities of coal from southern and Central Alberta that will keep for months and months, for an entire year if you like, in ordinary storage; in a basement this coal will keep almost for an indefinite period. Some of the northern coals do not possess the same keeping qualities. However, the reason I have given is not the only one why such a restriction should not apply, at least to western Canada. I have another reason to cite in opposition to it. We consume immense quantities of coal in western Canada,, and at the time the people have usually been filling up their bins with coal they have also been moving their wheat out. That works all right in so far as bringing in the anthracite coal is concerned; they can take that back in the cars from Fort William and Port Arthur, and it does not make so much difference. But when it comes to taking cars for the Alberta coal it is an entirely different matter, and the amount of power and the number of cars used during the months of October and November corresponds to about the power and cars required to move anywhere from eight to twelve million bushels of wheat to the head of the lakes. You will, therefore, see how important the restriction in question is from that viewpoint, apart altogether from securing a

supply of fuel for the winter months. We had a serious situation in Western Canada some time ago, just as serious, if not more so, than you had here in Ontario last winter, and we have only prevented a recurrence of it by endeavouring to get our people to secure their supply of coal during the months of June, July and August. That surely should apply this year more than at any time in the past. Without doubt, immediately wheat starts to move in western Canada this year, not one particle of power, nor any cars, should be used in handling coal that could be avoided.
As I stated a minute ago, I have absolutely no objection whatever to bringing in mining machinery free.
Mining machinery has been on the free list for ten or fifteen years.

I am glad to know it; it helps to make the argument all the stronger. There are a lot of other things that also ought to be free of duty. If it is a good thing to bring in the implements of one industry free in order to stimulate it, the principle should apply all the way round. I am very glad, indeed, to know that.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to get back into the matter of protection at all. But our protectionist people are always ready to remove the protection on everything that comes their particular way. I will just give you one illustration. I was talking to a British Columbia fruit grower, and incidentally the matter of protection on fruit came up, and he wanted to know what the western members were going to do about it. Perhaps he had been a little terrorized, I am not sure, but he had an idea that we were going to do something in the matter of duties. I told him that I did not know what they were going to do. He said: " You can remove the duty on any old thing you like, but for heaven's sake don't touch fruit." He was an absolute free trader so long as free trade did not apply to fruit. If it did, he immediately switched around. That is about the position we are in in western Canada, in so far as the fuel situation is concerned. All that we are asking is that the Government will at least demonstrate that the large and almost inexhaustible lignite coal fields in southern 'Saskatchewan can be put on the map as a commercial industry in order that we may not be entirely dependent on American anthracite coal to heat our homes during the winter. We must have either anthracite, or a substitute for it, a fuel that will keep up a continuous
[Mr. Maharg.}
fire anywhere from sixteen to twenty-four hours.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard several hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan, Ontario and British Columbia speak on this coal question, some of them offering their coal to the province of Quebec and to the other provinces of the Dominion which have no coal mines. After listening to these hon. gentlemen, I ask myself if they have made any practical suggestion in the course of their long or short speeches. Has it occurred to this Government, which seems to want to take charge of everything, to pass even, an Order in Council to relieve the city of Montreal from a fuel shortage? I am speaking particularly of soft coal. The industries of Montreal depend on the mines of the Maritime Provinces for their supply of coal. They are compelled to bring in this coal during the season of navigation, although we know that just across the line, as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) has said, only an imaginary line, there is coal. I am going to make a -constructive suggestion: why not blot out this imaginary line during the war? Are we not at war equally with the United States? If so, let us help one another. In -this way we may save the situation and relieve Montreal of the problem of a coal shortage such as it had last winter. I propose, as a practical proposition, the removal of the duty during
10 p.m. the war, so that we can get from the other side of the imaginary line the coal to satisfy the industries of Canada. I say that Montreal is suffering to-day from shortage of coal. We are paying more for gas and for light on account of this shortage. And we look to this Government, this Government of great men, to do something practical by blotting out this duty during the war. That is all I am going to say, because I do not want to be accused of making a -long speech. But we are expecting something practical from the Government in the sense of what I have been talking about.
Mr. ROBERT H. BUTTS (Cape Breton South and Richmond):	Mr. Speaker, I
think that British Columbia fruit grower, to whom my hon. friend (Mr. Maharg) referred a little while ago, who was satisfied to have free trade in everything but fruit, is typical of free traders, and, in reply to my hon. friend (Mr. L. A. Lapointe), who has just referred to Montreal and the coal situation there, let me ask him to recall the situation with respect to coal in the

city of Montreal eome few years ago. In the year when Mr. Fielding and the late Mr. Paterson went down to Washington to negotiate the reciprocity treaty, in the month of April, the city of Montreal called for tenders for the eupply of coal for the city for one year. The Dominion Coal Company was the only Canadian tenderer. There were one or more American tenderers, and the city of Montreal bought its coal from the American tenderer that year at 31 cents a ton less than the Dominion Coal Company's tender, so I do not think Montreal is suffering so very much from this "imaginary line."
Now, I have been struck by a number of statements that were made by these free traders, and it was only when they announced themselves as such that I thought they were free traders, for they did not argue along those lines. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) says that trade is the basis of wealth. That may be. But how are you going to trade if you do not produce? I think production is at the bottom of the whole matter. I think my hon. friend has forgotten a few of the principles that he learned from Adam Smith, and it is pretty nearly time for him to reread the Wealth of Nations. I think, Mr. Speaker, when we come to consider the whole matter, as far as eastern Nova Scotia is concerned, there are one or two things that are at the bottom of our declining production. One is the matter of transportation. I know myself that, in the month of June, 1917, the Dominion Coal Company were in straits as to shipping. A certain amount of their shipping had been commandeered for war purposes, and I know that they were making very,' very strong appeals to the Government of the day to have returned a number of their ships in order that they might transport their coal up the St. Lawrence. It is true that that may not have hampered production at the time; that might not have been the immediate cause of the slackening production, because at the time a large number of their men had enlisted, so that the Dominion Coal Company lost some thousands of employees, and perhaps had all their men remained there, together with the commandeering, the situation might have been very much more serious. The only reason in the world why they have not suffered during tlhe two last years for the want of shipping, is simply that into Sydney Harbour comes a very, very large amount of shipping. Almost every week or so, thirty, thirty-one, and, as high as thirty-nine, ships, varying
in tonnage from 7,000 to 17,000 tons, assemble there to be convoyed across the ocean. These ships all fill their bunkers there. Therefore, the question of transportation was not such a very serious one during the last year or two. "
